The first Flight II San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock completed builder’s sea trials over the weekend, Ingall’s Shipbuilding announced Tuesday.

The future USS Harrisburg (LPD-30) completed the multi-day trials on Saturday, during which Ingalls Shipbuilding tested the ship’s propulsion, steering and communications, as well as the ship-control, mission and combat systems. The ship now has to undergo acceptance trials before its delivery to the Navy later this year, reads the release from HII.

Ingalls Shipbuilding launched Harrisburg just over two years ago in October of 2024.

“This successful sea trial is a critical step toward delivering this ship to the fleet and a testament to the quality of our shipbuilders’ work,” Stephen Janowski, Ingalls Shipbuilding amphibious ship program manager, said in the release. “LPD-30 will provide the Navy and the Marine Corps with enhanced capability for generations, and we are proud to see the ship progressing so strongly toward delivery.”

Harrisburg is the first of three Flight II San Antonio-class LPDs under construction at Ingalls Shipbuilding in Pascagoula, Miss. The future USS Pittsburgh (LPD-31) and USS Philadelphia (LPD-32) are also at the shipyard while Ingalls plans to construct the future USS Travis Manion (LPD-33) and the next two LPDs.

Travis Manion, LPD-34 and LPD-35 are part of a $9.6 billion multi-year deal between the Navy and HII that also includes America-class big deck amphibious warship Helmand Province (LHA-10). The total cost, when including government furnished equipment, comes out to $11.5 billion, USNI News previously reported.

The deal follows a Pentagon study looking at Flight II LPDs’ capability and cost and a previous pause on buying amphibious ships.

The Royal Navy and Royal Air Force tracked Russian ships operating near the U.K. over three operations spanning a two-week period last month, the services announced Monday.

Royal Navy destroyer HMS Dauntless (D33), offshore patrol vessel HMS Tyne (P281) shadowed Russian Navy frigate RFS Neustrashimy (177) from Oct. 1-14 as the Russian ship escorted sanctioned cargo ships through the English Channel. Monitoring of Neustrashimy was conducted as part of three focused operations carried out by the Royal Navy, the service said in a news release.

“HMS Dauntless maintained the close and proficient monitoring of the Russian warship Neustrashimy during her operations within the English Channel, providing reassurance to the U.K. and our allies whilst contributing to a comprehensive understanding of the maritime environment that surrounds us. I am immensely proud of the professionalism, dedication and operational readiness displayed by every member of HMS Dauntless throughout this tasking,”said Cmdr. Neil Skinner, commanding officer of Dauntless.

In a second operation Tyne monitored Russian amphibious landing ship RFS Aleksandr Shabalin (110) as it escorted Russian flagged cargo ship MV Energy-2 (IMO1076850) and Russian flagged tugboat Proton (IMO1054400) during their transit of the English Channel towards the Baltic region. Tyne and a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron monitored the passage of the Russian ships from Oct. 11-14.

“Maintaining a persistent presence around the U.K. and beyond, we stand ready to respond at a moment’s notice to protect our nation’s interests. I am proud of my ship’s company for their unwavering professionalism and adaptability,” said Lt. Cmdr. Sam Fields, Tyne’s commanding officer.

Merlin helicopters from Royal Naval Air Station (RNAS) Culdrose in Cornwall were deployed at short notice to Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. From Sept. 29-Oct. 8, the helicopters kept track of Russian surveillance ship Viktor Leonov (175) in the Outer Hebrides. The Russian ship was believed to be monitoring NATO warships taking part in Exercise Strike Warrior off the coast of Scotland.

Capt. James Hall, the commanding officer of RNAS Culdrose, said that the tasking was part of a wider series of operations, known collectively as Operation Iceblast. Operation Iceblast was designed to test the ability of the Merlin Helicopter Force to deploy away from its home base of RNAS Culdrose in force and at short notice.

“This operation has been a critical means for demonstrating to ourselves, our adversaries and the nation that we are willing and capable of securing the homeland 24/7. The Merlin Helicopter Force stands ready to answer the call at a moment’s notice,” Hall said.

On Monday, the Royal Air Force announced that its Protector RG1 unmanned aerial vehicle recently conducted 10 hours of persistent Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) coverage, monitoring Russian naval activity around the U.K. The flight was the first operational sortie in U.K. airspace, according to the announcement.

“Working alongside Royal Navy warships and helicopters, Protector demonstrated its ability to deliver long-endurance surveillance and operate seamlessly within busy U.K. airspace, strengthening the U.K.’s ability to monitor activity in areas of national interest,” reads the Facebook post.

The announcement did not disclose when the flight occurred but the post included a photo of Neustrashimy. The post also included a photo of a KA-27 helicopter on the flight deck of the frigate that was taken by the UAV.

The RAF has a program of record for 16 Protectors, which is based on the MQ-9B SkyGuardian. The Protector also has weapons capability with the Brimstone missile and Paveway IV 500-pound precision guided bomb.

Russian activity around the U.K. and in the North Atlantic has risen 25 percent in the first half of the year compared to the same time frame in 2025, USNI News reported in August. An average of two Royal Navy warships deploy each week to monitor Russian ships operating in U.K.’s maritime domain, according to First Sea Lord Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, who said in September that Russia is the greatest threat to the U.K.’s national security.

“We know that Russia is probing us for weakness. And we are facing threats…in a way we have not been since the Cold War,” Jenkins said at the time.

The following is Canada’s first national security strategy in over 20 years, “The Plan for a Stronger Canada,” released Oct. 29. 2026.

From the Report

Message from the Prime Minister Mark Carney

This is the plan for a sovereign, resilient, and prosperous Canada.

It has been over 20 years since Canada last published a national security policy. Today’s world demands a new plan that reflects profound new realities.

Canada stands at a hinge moment in history.

The world is increasingly defined by contested borders, authoritarian aggression, and acute global threats. The long-held belief that the combination of our geography, interconnectedness, and a rules-based international order could substitute for Canadian sovereign capacity to protect ourselves is no longer tenable.

Threats once thought distant are now immediate and proximate. The international rules-based order is under threat. The open global trading system is deeply challenged. What were once strengths—our strong connections and deep integration with other countries—have become vulnerabilities.

To bolster our sovereignty and national security, we will build long-term economic strength through generational domestic investments. We will develop a dense web of trading relationships that bolster our strategic capabilities. We will focus our diplomatic efforts on practical cooperation and partnerships that will help us influence the course of global events to serve the interests of Canadians. We will rebuild, rearm, and reinvest in the Canadian Armed Forces. We will develop our sovereign defense industrial capabilities. We will collect actionable intelligence. We will continue to invest in keeping our borders secure and stopping criminals. We will live up to our responsibility to defend Canada’s Arctic in support of Canadian, North American, and global security.

The Plan for a Stronger Canada puts forward an ambitious vision: A Canada that controls its own destiny and is resilient in the face of daunting challenges.

The Strategy requires clear priorities and unprecedented focus by the Government of Canada. Fortunately, the new reality plays to Canada’s strengths: our people, our resources, and our principles. Canadian energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, and leading technologies will be the bedrock of our relationships that promote a sovereign Canada and contribute to a more secure and prosperous world.

item.content:encoded:
The Chinese Navy’s new Type 076 drone carrier launched and recovered a stealthy unmanned combat aerial vehicle for the first time last week in the service’s latest effort to bring the new vessel online.

Sichuan (51) carried out flight operations with the GJ-21 stealth reconnaissance-strike drone, according to a People’s Liberation Army Navy news release on Friday. Aside from a graphic, no media of the event has been released.

“Since beginning its maiden sea trial in November 2025, Sichuan has steadily conducted a series of scheduled maritime tests, successfully completing the commissioning of its onboard systems and equipment, as well as comprehensive assessments of its overall operational stability,” reads the PLAN release.

Since Sichuan’s launch in 2024, the Type 076 amphibious assault ship has engaged in a variety of trials and work-up drills. The 40,000-ton drone carrier held its first sea trials last fall and has been spotted with mock UCAVs on its flight deck. This class builds on the PLAN’s Type 075 landing helicopter deck with dedicated facilities for unmanned aerial system missions. Upgrades include an electromagnetic drone catapult and a tower for aviation operations.

The sole Type 076 is China’s first foray into the drone carrier concept, which has been on the rise in recent years across a variety of nations. Beijing’s GJ-21 UCAV also brings a low-observable intelligence and strike platform to the PLAN’s naval aviation roster. Drones from Sichuan can be used in support of its embarked PLAN Marine Corps complement or the PLANAF’s growing carrier strike groups. However, it is unclear how the service will field the GJ-21 within operations and doctrine.

Sichuan’s potential is one of several significant vectors pursued by Beijing in its expansive UAV development, integration and research efforts. In 2025, a concept from Chinese defense manufacturers showcased how containerized systems can rapidly militarize cargo ships. These capabilities included air defense systems, cruise missiles and a configurable electromagnetic catapult that can support drone launches. This concept was highlighted at Sichuan’s yard in Shanghai aboard container ship Zhongda 79.

In the Western Pacific, Chinese WZ-7s UAVs are a common sight around Taiwan, Japan and the South China Sea. The PLA Air Force is working to field several Collaborative Combat Aircraft concepts that will be commanded via twin-seater J-20 5th-generation fighters.

item.content:encoded:
The hulk of former nuclear aircraft carrier USS Enterprise (CVN-65) was towed from a pier at Newport News Shipbuilding on Monday, almost 15 years after its final deployment, USNI News has learned.

“Ex-Enterprise began its final transit this morning, departing Newport News Shipbuilding for Mobile, Alabama, where the ship will be dismantled,” reads a Monday statement from PAE Maritime.

The remnant “Big E” is now in route to Mobile, Ala., after a court battle between environmental disposal contractor NorthStar and HII over which company would oversee the final disposal. Last month, HII dropped a legal challenge on the Navy’s decision to award NorthStar $418 million for the disposal work.

“We’re creating a blueprint for the Navy on how to dispose of [carriers],” PMS 386 commander of the Nuclear-Powered Aircraft Carrier Inactivation and Disposal Program Office (PMS 368) Capt. William Cleveland said in a 2024 statement. “It’s exciting work that will shape standards across the Navy’s nuclear enterprise.”

HII was responsible for the initial inactivation and defueling of the carrier until this year’s award. Removing the remaining reactors, disposing of the radioactive materials and dismantling the ship will be a major challenge due to the eight of reactors aboard. In contrast, the Nimitz and Ford-class carriers each have two.

“For submarines, you remove the reactor compartment as an entire section and ship it off to a disposal site,” Naval analyst Bryan Clark told USNI News in July. “That’s difficult enough, but it’s straightforward. Here, the reactor compartment is too big, so you have to disassemble the hull itself.”

Up until now, HII was the primary contractor responsible for defueling the 94,000-ton carrier before NorthStar won the contract in July.

The Navy has spent about $1.3 billion on the total inactivation of Enterprise, USNI News reported earlier this year.

HII referred comment on the hulk’s move to the Navy.

item.content:encoded:
Marine Rotational Force-Southeast Asia is now on its second continuous rotation to the Philippines, the service announced last week.

MRF-SEA held a rotation turnover on Oct. 26. MRF-SEA originally began as a six-month rotational force that deployed to the region from October to March but its mission was extended in April. The force is now providing a continuous presence in the Philippines at the invitation of the country’s government to continue cooperation with its military.

MRF-SEA is one of two rotational forces operating under the aegis of I Marine Expeditionary Force, with the other being Marine Rotational Force-Darwin. Unlike MRF-D, which deploys as a Marine Air-Ground Task Force, MRF-SEA deploys as a scalable task force with its command headquarters being the permanent component. Other Marine units are assigned as and when required.

Before the rotation extension, the command element of the MRF-SEA would move between Southeast Asian countries based on where scheduled activities would take place. Since April, the command element has been based in the Philippines

The current deployment is the sixth iteration of MRF-SEA. The rotational deployment began in 2022. The unit’s presence is designed to strengthen combined readiness and the U.S.-Philippine Alliance, according to a Marine Corps news release, with each rotation building on the relationships and lessons of the force before in an approach MRF-SEA calls “presence with purpose.”

“Our goal was never simply to be present in the Philippines,” said Col. Robert Bunn, commanding officer of the outgoing MRF-SEA rotation. “Presence has to have purpose. Every exercise, planning session and repetition alongside our Philippine allies was an opportunity to become more interoperable, responsive and capable together, progressively getting better with each event. The next rotation now has the opportunity to take those lessons and relationships to move the alliance another step forward.”

The previous rotation of MRF-SEA saw the force train alongside Philippine troops during Balikatan 26, KAMANDAG 10 and a series of bilateral events through the Archipelagic Coastal Defense Continuum (ACDC). The continuum provided recurring training between major exercises, allowing U.S. and Philippine forces to apply lessons from one event to the next. ACDC is is a series of bilateral training activities and subject matter expert exchanges that support Philippine Marine Corps modernization efforts and the Philippine Marine Corps’ Archipelagic Coastal Defense Concept along with strengthening combined readiness between U.S. and Philippine forces

Training throughout the previous MRF-SEA rotation included command and control, sensing, fires integration, maritime domain awareness, aviation, communications and unmanned systems.

Marines also tested how forces and equipment could move, communicate and operate across the Philippines’ distributed and archipelagic terrain. This included testing the mobility of the AN/TPS-80 Ground/Air Task-Oriented Radar as part of ACDC training and movement of the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) from ports to distributed exercise locations as part of KAMANDAG 10.

The incoming rotation will continue the progression of the U.S.-Philippine partnership through ACDC and Exercise Balikatan 27, according to the release. Training will continue to focus on operating across distributed and archipelagic terrain, strengthening the ability of U.S. and Philippine forces to coordinate, maneuver and sustain operations across geographically dispersed locations. Marines and sailors will also continue bilateral humanitarian assistance, disaster response and crisis response training.

“Our Marines and sailors are inheriting more than a mission, they are inheriting momentum,” said Col. Coby Moran, commanding officer of the incoming MRF-SEA rotation. “We will build on the relationships, lessons and interoperability developed by the Marines and sailors before us and continue working shoulder-to-shoulder with our Philippine allies.”

Moran previously operated in the Philippines, leading a I MEF technical assistance and advisory team in April that oversaw a maritime prepositioning force offload at the Port of Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, Philippines. The event was the first MPF offload at Mindanao, according to a Marine Corps news release at the time.

The offload saw roll-on/roll-off cargo ship USNS Sgt. William W. Seay (T-AKR-302) transport vehicles and equipment to I MEF, which was preparing for Exercise Balikatan 26 in the Philippines.

“MPF operations are a unique capability of the Marine Corps,” said Moran in the release. “They allow us to deliver capabilities anywhere in the world, providing critical combat power to Marine air-ground task force commanders.”

The Marine Corps has not disclosed whether MRF-SEA will now only focus on the Philippines or whether it will continue leading Marine Corps engagement and activities with other countries in the region alongside its activities in the Philippines.

Russia and North Korea carried out ballistic missile launches this week with Russia conducting a launch of a Submarine-Launched Ballistic Missile (SLBM) from the Western Pacific to Russia arctic region, according to a Russian Ministry of Defence (MOD) release on Wednesday while North Korea carried out launches of Short-Range Ballistic Missiles (SRBMs) as part of a firepower demonstration for North Korea leader Kim Jong Un during an exhibition of unmanned aerial vehicle technology.

Nuclear powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) RFS Generalissimus Suvorov (K-553), assigned to the Russian Navy Pacific Fleet, launched a RSM-56 Bulava SLBM from the sea of Okhotsk at the Chizha test site in the Arkhangelsk region of northwest Russia.

“The strategic nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Generalissimus Suvorov launched a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile in accordance with the combat training plan,”the Russian MOD said on Wednesday. The missiles were fired from a submerged position and the missile’s warheads successfully reached the designated area at the estimated time. The Russian MOD also released a video of the launch that was carried by state media TASS.

The Russian MOD did not state when the launch took place though international navigational warnings were issued on missile activity being carried out from Oct. 25-31. Russia has regularly carried out SLBM launches from the Russian Far East during the October to November with Generalissimus Suvorov firing a Bulava on Nov. 3 2022 prior to being commissioned on Dec. 29 that year, reported USNI News.

Russia last carried out an SLBM launch by a SSBN on May 21 this year when a submerged Delta IV class SSBN launched an R-29RMU Sineva SLBM as part of an exercise of its strategic nuclear forces. There has been only two other publicly disclosed SLBM launches this year, with China carrying out a launch in July from the South China Sea into the South Pacific and France carrying out one in early October, launching an SLBM from off the coast of Finistère, France into a remote area of the North Atlantic. Unlike Russia, where the SLBM landed in national territory and France, where it landed in the North Atlantic, several hundred kilometers from any coastline, China was criticised by South Pacific island states and other countries for using the area as an SLBM test site.

North Korea on Thursday conducted firings of its KN-25 600mm multiple launch rockets, which are classed as SRBMs, as part of a firepower demonstration during an exhibition of UAV technology that was attended by North Korea leader Kim Jong Un.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff on Thursday stated that North Korea launched 10 short range ballistic missiles (SRBMs) from Wonsan into the Sea of Japan at 12.30 p.m. local time, the JCS also said the SRBMs flew for a distance of 250km. Japan’s Ministry of Defense (MOD) reported on Thursday that North Korea launched a ballistic missile at 12.36 p.m. that day and it was estimated that the ballistic missile landed near the east coast of the Korean Peninsula. Both the JSC and MOD stated that the U.S., Japan and South Korea were sharing information and analysing the launches. U.S. Pacific Command’s meanwhile placed the number of ballistic missiles launched at two in its statement.

On Friday, state media Korean Central News Agency reported that Kim visited the Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026 exhibition on Thursday, which showcase North Korea’s UAV capabilities and advancements. KCNA did not state the location of the exhibition though it was likely in Wonsan given the SRBM launches from the area on Thursday matched what was fired during the firepower demonstration.

In his speech at the exhibition, Kim called on North Korea to seize absolute superiority in drone technology and urged North Korean scientists to go all out in obtaining miraculous results in research on UAV and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for national defence. After touring the exhibition, the North Korean leader witnessed a firepower demonstration that involved strikes on islet target by various tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multi-purpose drones and a 600mm-calibre Multiple Rocket Launcher (MRL) battalion. KCNA also reported that the demonstration also involved the first publicly displayed firing of a 600mm-calibre ultra-precision MRL called ‘Sniper’.

The rockets fired by North Korea’s KN-25 MRL are classed as SRBMs and North Korea has claimed they can be fitter with nuclear warheads. Imagery by KCNA, showed salvo firings by a dozen launchers. KCNA also released images showing UAVs launching missiles and loitering munitions hitting targets with some of the targets made to look like South Korean outpost and K9 Thunder Self-Propelled Howitzers and U.S. M1 Abrams tanks.

KCNA images also showed Kim looking at racks of First Person View (FPV) Small Unmanned Aerial Systems (SUASs) and a new flying wing stealth design UAV not previously seen. The state media did not report or provided any details on the UAVs shown. It is unclear as to whether the flying wing UAV was an operational UAV or a model representing an actual in service UAV or one under development.

The following is a summary of major ship movements and exercises in the Western Pacific over the last week. 

Around Japan

Aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) conducted a passenger exchange on Monday with Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina (FFH 334) during exercise Keen Sword 27 (KS27). The U.S.-Japan bilateral Exercise Keen Sword 27 closed on Thursday, having begun on Oct. 19 with the majority of activities taking place in Japan’s southwest region. 

The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group consists of aircraft carrier Theodore Roosevelt with embarked carrier air wing (CVW) 11, cruiser USS Chosin (CG-65) and destroyers USS Paul Hamilton (DDG-60) and USS Decatur (DDG-73).

Earlier on Saturday, Theodore Roosevelt carried out a replenishment-at-sea with fleet oiler USNS Tippecanoe (T-AO-199) as part of the exercise.

Although a bilateral exercise between the U.S and Japan, partner nations were invited to participate. Approximately 45,000 members from the Japan Self-Defense Force, 11,000 U.S. service members and an unknown number of forces from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines participated alongside observers from the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom. 

A total of 260 aircraft and 40 ships, including the Theodore Roosevelt CSG were deployed in the drills. Exercise activities included force-on-force drills between 12th Marine Littoral Regiment (MLR) and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force at JGSDF Hijudai Maneuver Area, Kyushu on Sunday, maritime operations in Okinawa by Expeditionary Operations Training Group and 3rd Reconnaissance Battalion, 3rd Marine Division on Monday and bilateral convoys operations in Okinawa between 3rd Landing Support Battalion, 3rd Marine Logistics Group and the JGSDF on Monday.

In the Philippine Sea

The Liaoning Carrier Strike Group is operating in the Philippine Sea east of the Philippine main island of Luzon as of Wednesday according to a graphic posted by Joseph Wu, Secretary General of Taiwan’s National Security Council. The strike group includes aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16) cruisers CNS Anshan (101) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainan (123).

In Yokosuka, Japan

The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group pulled into Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka (CFAY) on Monday for maintenance and resupply. The ARG includes amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island (LHD-8), amphibious transport docks USS Anchorage (LPD-23) and USS John P. Murtha (LPD-26) and the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).

Cruiser USS Chosin (CG-65), part of the Theodore Roosevelt CSG pulled into CFAY on Sunday and departed on Wednesday, according to local ship spotters.

Destroyer USS Howard (DDG-83) returned home to CFAY on Saturday, according to local ship spotters

The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force training squadron returned home to JMSDF Yokosuka Naval Base on Saturday, completing a 161-day training cruise. The squadron, which included training ship JS Kashima (TV-3508) and training ship/destroyer JS Yamagiri (TV-3515), sailed to Iceland, Canada and participated in the International Naval Review (INR) 250 in New York.

Expeditionary fast transport USNS City of Bismarck (T-EPF-9) and Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Stuart (FFH153) docked into Yokosuka on Friday according to local ship spotters.

In the Miyako Strait

On Tuesday, a single Chinese Y-9 Electronic Intelligence (ELINT) aircraft flew in from the East China Sea and passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. The aircraft flew as far as south of Amami Oshima, then flew back to return to the East China Sea. Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighter aircraft of the Southwestern Air Defense Command were scrambled to intercept the Y-9.

Also on Tuesday, People’s Liberation Army Navy cruiser CNS Lhasa (102) and fleet oiler CNS Kekexilihu (903) were sighted sailing southeast 140 kilometers – 87 miles – northeast of Miyako Island and subsequently sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. 

A JMSDF P-3C Orion Maritime Patrol Aircraft shadowed the PLAN ships.

That same day, PLAN destroyer CNS Xining (117) and frigate CNS Yanchang (546) were spotted south 70 kilometers – 43 miles – west of Kume Island. The ships subsequently sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea while under surveillance by a JMSDF P-3C Orion MPA of Fleet Air Wing 5.

On Wednesday, a Chinese Y-9 ELINT and a BZK-005 reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle flew in from the East China Sea and passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. The aircraft and drone flew to the northeast before turning back and returning the same way into the East China Sea. The JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command scrambled fighter aircraft in response.

On Thursday, a Chinese TB-001 reconnaissance UAV flew in from the East China Sea and over the waters between Miyako Island and Okinawa to enter the Philippine Sea. The drone then flew northeast and conducted a patrol circuit before returning back to the East China Sea the same way.

Also on Thursday, a Y-9 MPA flew in from the East China Sea, and also passed over the waters between Miyako Island and Okinawa to enter the Philippine Sea. The Y-9 then flew northeast before subsequently returning to the East China Sea. JASDF fighter aircraft from the Southwestern Air Defense Command were launched in response.

In the East China Sea

On Wednesday, a Chinese Y-9 MPA flew in from China to an area southwest of the Danjo Islands in the East China Sea then to an area northwest of Okinawa before returning towards China. Fighter aircraft from the JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command were scrambled to intercept the Y-9.

In the Osumi Strait

A joint PLAN/China Coast Guard task group was sighted sailing east 200 kilometers – 124 miles – west of Kuchinoerabu Island at 10 a.m. on Tuesday and subsequently sailed east through the Osumi Strait, which separates the main island of Kyushu and Tanegashima Island, to enter the Pacific Ocean. The group included cruiser CNS Dongguan (109), destroyer CNS Baotou (133), frigate CNS Xuzhou (530) and China Coast Guard ship CCG 2307. 

JMSDF destroyer JS Shiranui (DD-120), minesweeper JS Takashima (MSC-603) and a JMSDF P-1 MPA shadowed the Chinese ships, according to a Japan Joint Staff Office news release. The release also marks the first time Japan has announced that a China Coast Guard ship is operating with PLAN ships around Japan.

PLAN Dongdiao-class surveillance ship Yuhengxing (798) sailed west through the Osumi Strait to enter the East China Sea on Thursday. It had earlier been sighted at 2 p.m. sailing west in an area 60 kilometers southeast of Cape Toi on the main island of Kyushu. JMSDF destroyer JS Kongo (DDG-173) and destroyer JS Abukuma (DE-229) shadowed the PLAN ship. Yuhengxing on Oct. 17-18. had transited east through the Osumi Strait to enter the Pacific Ocean

In the Tsushima Strait

Russian Navy surveillance ship Kareliya (535) transited southwest through the Tsushima Strait between Tuesday and Wednesday to enter the East China Sea. The Russia ship was previously sighted sailing southwest on Tuesday around 80 kilometers – 50 miles – northeast of Tsushima. JMSDF minesweeper JS Hirashima (MSC-601) and a JMSDF P-1 MPA from Fleet Air Wing 4 monitored the Russian ship.

In the Sea of Okhotsk

Russian nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) RFS Generalissimus Suvorov (K-553) launched a Bulava Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) at the Chizha test site in the Arkhangelsk region of northwest Russia, the Russian Defense Ministry announced on Wednesday. The Ministry also released a video of the launch. The video, by state media Tass, shows the ICBM being launched from the submarine while it was submerged.

At Kunsan Air Base, South Korea

The U.S. Air Force and Republic of Korea Air Force began two weeks of airpower drills on Monday under Exercise Freedom Flag 26-2, a biannual exercise designed to enhance the interoperability of U.S.-ROK allied forces, strengthening response capabilities and contributing to regional stability.

In Wonsan, North Korea

North Korea launched 10 short range ballistic missiles (SRBMs) from Wonsan into the Sea of Japan at 12.30 p.m. local time Thursday, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The SRBMs flew for a distance of 250 kilometers – 155 miles.

Thursday’s launches appeared to be from a firepower demonstration on the same day for North Korea leader Kim Jong Un at an exhibition on unmanned technology in an undisclosed location as photographs by state media Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) showed salvo firing of North Korea’s 600mm multiple rocket launcher whose rockets are classed as SRBMs during the demonstration.

In the South China Sea

The Armed Forces of the Philippines, Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, and U.S. Coast Guard conducted a multi-lateral Maritime Cooperative Activity (MCA) within the Philippine Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the South China Sea on Saturday. 

The Philippines deployed Philippine Navy frigate BRP Diego Silang (FFG-07) and a Philippine Navy AW159 Wildcat helicopter, Philippine Coast Guard patrol vessel BRP Suluan (MRRV-4406) and a Philippine Air Force C208 Caravan aircraft to carry out drills with JMSDF destroyer JS Kirisame (DD-104) and U.S. Coast Guard cutter USCGC Bertholf (WMSL-750).

“This activity continues to showcase our demonstrated, collective commitment to strengthening regional and international cooperation in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific,” reads a U.S. 7th Fleet news release on the activity.

In the Malacca Strait

Littoral combat ship USS Charleston (LCS-18) was operating in the Malacca Strait on Sunday. Charleston is on a scheduled deployment operating in the U.S. 7th Fleet area of operations and is assigned to Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 7.

In Western Australia

Fast attack submarine USS Colorado (SSN-788) arrived at HMAS Stirling, Western Australia, on Tuesday to begin a scheduled month-long maintenance period. The visit marks the fourth submarine maintenance period in Western Australia since the establishment of AUKUS.

This post was written by Dzirhan Mahadzir.

Hanwha Philly Shipyard has won a $269 million contract to build the Marine Corps’ Landing Ship Medium, according to a Friday announcement from the program’s vessel construction manager.

TOTE Services, which won a $2.2 billion contract in July to function as the LSM vessel construction manager, awarded Hanwha the contract after putting out a request for proposals in July.

“Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) is the first shipbuilder selected through that process, based on its competitive pricing and acceptance of TOTE Services’ subcontract terms and conditions,” reads a TOTE news release. “The award covers construction of one LSM, valued at $269 million, at Hanwha Philly Shipyard (HPSI), with options for three additional vessels.”

Gulf Coast-based Bollinger Shipyards is already on contract to build the first LSM. Fincantieri Marinette Marine out of Wisconsin won a contract earlier this year for long lead items for four ships.

TOTE’s LSM contract is for as many as eight ships, according to the company.

“TOTE Services continues productive contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, both directed shipyards under the VCM contract, which are expected to play a meaningful role in building the LSM fleet,” reads the release.

This is the first time the Navy has opted to use a vessel construction manager, which runs the program on behalf of the service.

The LSM program has faced years of requirements churn as the Navy and Marine Corps debated the ship’s design and survivability. The platform is a crucial component of the Marine Corps’ current strategy for countering China in the Western Pacific, where smaller units of Marines would move around between islands and shorelines to set up ad-hoc bases from which they could fire anti-ship missiles.

The LSM is based on the Damen LST-100 concept, an export-oriented tank landing ship design currently in service with the Nigerian Navy and also planned for the Royal Australian Navy. The Navy bought the design package for $17 million, USNI News previously reported.

TOTE is already managing another program under construction at Hanwha Philly Shipyard – the U.S. Maritime Administration’s National Security Multi-Mission Vessel.

Last year, the White House announced the outlines of a trade deal with South Korea following President Donald Trump’s visit to the country. That deal included a pledge from South Korea to put $150 billion into American shipbuilding.

It will take a couple years before deployment lengths shift from the extended 10-11 months back to the normal seven, the Navy’s top enlisted sailor said Wednesday. 

As sailors deploy with carrier strike groups, they are being told to expect a deployment that is between 10-11 months, MCPON John Perryman said while speaking at the Navy Memorial. 

The longer extensions started in 2023 with the Dwight D. Eisenhower Carrier Strike Group seeing a nine-month deployment as a result of the Houthi campaign in the Red Sea. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran in late February, the operations began a cycle of deployments that extended past 11 months. 

The Gerald R. Ford CSG spent 326 days at sea, which included time in the Middle East – the third longest deployment since 1972. The Abraham Lincoln CSG, which returned home Oct. 8, spent 321 days at sea, the bulk of which was in the Middle East. The Abraham Lincoln CSG deployment was the fourth longest deployment since 1972, and it also broke the record for longest days at sea.

Now, the Navy is telling its sailors to expect the longer deployments in an attempt to send them out with realistic expectations of deployment length, Perryman said. 

“Nobody wants an 11 month deployment. Everybody understands that,” Perryman said. “But what they really don’t like is getting told it’s seven months, and then every two weeks getting a change. It’s the uncertainty. They can’t plan for it.” 

The Navy does not want the long deployments either, Perryman said. Longer deployments often mean longer maintenance, messing with the Navy’s availability cycles. 

The sailors will do longer deployments, as long as there is a port call, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said during a talk at the Navy Memorial on Tuesday. USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) went 265 days at-sea, the longest a Navy ship has gone without visiting a port.

“They need to take a knee, and if you’re going to hold them at sea for seven, eight, nine, 10, 11 months, then they got to be able to take a knee,” Caudle said. “And the port call doesn’t have to be that glamorous, but it needs to be able to pull in, let them call home, let them get on dry land, and just do a little refresh, revive and get back in the fight again.”

When extensions come down from the Pentagon, the Navy submits a memo saying why the service does not think a longer deployment would be good, Perryman said. 

“The decision to extend to our ships longer is a decision above the Navy,” he said. “The president has a different calculus than we do, and so [the Pentagon makes] the decisions that they have to make, and then we support those decisions.” 

Caudle works with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine to figure out what the schedules will look like to bring more certainty for the sailors, he said. 

“You can kind of expect at least a 10-month deployment, and so that’s just the nature of what the capacity of the Navy can do,” Caudle said. “I need a bigger Navy, and if you want to shorten the length of time of deployments, then obviously the math would say I need more capacity.” 

Ships that are deploying now are going out to the Middle East with more supplies, Perryman said, following the issues faced by the Abraham Lincoln CSG as a result of the damage to the naval station in Bahrain. 

The sea service is also adjusting for the other side of deployment, when sailors who have been at sea for 10, 11 months are now back home, Perryman said. It can be a challenging time for sailors who have gone from having a set schedule and mission to more fluidity upon their arrival home, Matthew Brown, co-founder of Chimney Trail, which provides training for sailors using cognitive behavioral therapy, told USNI News earlier this month when the Abe CSG arrived home to San Diego. 

The loss of agency can be a challenge for a sailor’s mental health, Brown said. He flew out to Abe to speak with sailors as the ship headed back to San Diego.

Fleet and Family Services also have a handful of programs aimed at sailors returning from deployments, Brown said. 

After the longer deployments in the Red Sea, the Navy adjusted its programs to interact with sailors who returned, including identifying what a sailor’s risk level was, Perryman said. 

There are checkpoints in place every 30 days depending on the risk level, he said. 

On the other hand, the longer deployments are seeing sailors faced with re-enlistment sign up again, Perryman said. Of the sailors aboard Abe who had the choice to re-enlist, 74 percent did so. 

It is unclear how many sailors were up for reenlistment during the deployment. 

Abe, USS George Washington (CVN-73) and USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78) have the highest ship retention, Caudle said. The Navy also brought in 46,000 enlisted active-duty sailors in Fiscal Year 2026, he said. 

“They join to be in a combat service role, and that’s what they’re getting the opportunity to do,” Caudle said. 

Abe is now preparing to go to the shipyard, where the Navy sees its worst retention rates, Perryman said. 

“Sailors hate being in the shipyard,” he said. 

The Navy is working on creating more housing as one way to make quality of life better for the junior sailors whose ships are in the shipyard. There are about 1,000 sailors who still live on ships, down from 7,000, Caudle said. 

The Navy and Pentagon entered into a $1.7 billion contract with Hunt Military Communities to bring more beds to the Hampton Roads area, one of the highest fleet concentration areas without the available housing for junior sailors. 

Additionally, 90 percent of Navy barracks have wi-fi, with the remaining 10 percent in more remote areas, like Diego Garcia, Caudle said. Other pilot programs, run through Commander, Navy Installations Command, are focusing on bringing better food options to sailors.

The United States, Australia, India and Japan will carry out this year’s iteration of the annual Malabar naval exercise in the waters near Japan next week. 

Malabar 2026 will take place south of the Kanto region on the main island of Honshu from Nov. 5-12, according to a Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force news release published on Tuesday. 

“The JMSDF will conduct a multilateral exercise ‘MALABAR 2026’ with the U.S. Navy , the Indian Navy, the Royal Australian Navy and the Royal Australian Air Force as described below in order to realize a ‘Free and Open Indo-Pacific’,” reads the release.

The JMSDF will deploy helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182), frigate JS Mogami (FFM-1), a submarine and a P-1 Maritime Patrol Aircraft for the drills, according to the release. 

The Indian Navy will deploy frigate INS Sahyadri (F49), while Australia will deploy frigate HMAS Stuart (FFH153) and a Royal Australian Air Force P-8A Poseidon MPA. Both Stuart and the P-8A recently participated in the U.S.-Japan exercise Keen Sword 27, which wrapped up on Thursday.

The U.S. Navy will deploy a P-8A and an unidentified amphibious transport dock, the JMSDF release reads. 

There are currently four amphibious transport docks in Japan. USS New Orleans (LPD-18) and USS San Diego (LPD-22) are forward deployed to Japan at Commander Fleet Activities Sasebo (CFAS) as part of Amphibious Squadron 11 (PHIBRON 11). 

Amphibious transport docks USS Anchorage (LPD-23) and USS John P. Murtha (LPD-26) is currently docked at Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka (CFAY), having arrived there on Monday for a port visit. Anchorage and John P. Murtha, with amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island (LHD-8) and the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), form the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group.

Malabar 2026 drills will include: anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare drills and a joint sail photo exercise. 

Last year’s Malabar was hosted by the U.S. in Guam and saw U.S Navy destroyer USS Fitzgerald (DDG-62), a submarine and a P-8A training with Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Ballarat (FFH155), Sahyadri and JMSDF helicopter destroyer JS Hyuga (DDH-181).

Meanwhile Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom all wrapped up key exercises over last week.

Australia completed its participation in the Five Power Defense Arrangements Exercise Bersama Lima 2026 on Oct. 23 and the bilateral Australian-Indonesian Exercise Keris Woomera on Oct. 20.

Bersama Lima is an annual multi-domain exercise involving the militaries of the FPDA nations of Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore and the U.K. with Malaysia and Singapore alternating as the host for the exercise, which is held in the land, waters and airspaces of both countries. 

This year’s iteration was hosted by Singapore and ran from Oct. 5-23 with a total of 1,900 personnel. The exercise also included 42 aircraft, seven ships and one submarine. 

Naval assets participating included Royal Australian Navy fleet oiler HMAS Stalwart (A304), Republic of Singapore Navy frigate RSS Intrepid, littoral mission vessel RSS Dauntless (21) and an Invincible-class submarine, Royal Malaysian Navy corvette KD Lekir (FSG26) and offshore patrol vessel KD Pahang (172) and Royal Navy offshore patrol vessels HMS Tamar (P233) and HMS Spey (P234). 

Stalwart later joined the drills following its participation in Keris Woomera in Indonesia while the other FPDA ships docked into Changi Naval Base in Singapore prior to the shore phase of the exercise.

New Zealand did not deploy a ship for the maritime portion of the drills but participated through the Royal New Zealand Navy’s Deployable Boarding Team (DBT), which were embarked on Tamar to conduct boarding operations from the Royal Navy ship and a Royal New Zealand Air Force P-8A. The ship and aircraft participated in the combined anti-submarine exercise, which saw it and a Royal Australian Air Force P-8A operate alongside Lekir, Intrepid and the Republic of Singapore Navy submarine. 

Other naval drills included maneuvering exercises, naval gun firing, air defense exercises, boarding and diving serials.

The Royal Australian Air Force also deployed six F-35A fighters to operate alongside the RAAF and RNZAF P-8As, Republic of Singapore Air Force F-15SG and F-16 fighters and Multi-Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) aircraft and Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) F-18 and Su-30MKM fighters for the air portion of Bersama Lima. The air portion saw dissimilar air combat training, air defense scenarios, maritime air surveillance, air-to-air refuelling, fighter landaway, and casualty evacuation training being carried out. 

Land forces from the FPDA conducted professional exchanges and force integration training that culminated in a field exercise involving both jungle and urban environments.

From Oct. 12-20, Australia and Indonesia conducted Exercise Keris Woomera 26 in East Java, the Bali Sea and surrounding maritime areas with 1,000 Australian Defense Force personnel and more than 1,200 members of the Indonesian National Armed Forces. The forces carried out various drills, including amphibious landing operations, live-fire activities, maritime integration between Australian and Indonesian naval forces and combined air-land training serials.

Indonesian Navy corvette KRI Sultan Iskandar Muda (367) and RAN frigate HMAS Perth (FFH157), amphibious dock landing ship HMAS Choules (L100) and Stalwart operated as a joint naval task force for the drills. Choules deployed the Australian Amphibious Force, which worked alongside landing craft and a maritime tactical operations team to project and sustain combat power from sea to shore with the Indonesian Marine Corps.

Keris Woomera also saw live-fire engagements and joint artillery integration of Australian Army M777 155mm Howitzers and HIMARS with Indonesian 105mm Howitzers and multiple launch rocket systems. Close air support, forward air control and airlift missions were carried out by RAAF PC-21 and C-130J Hercules aircraft, operating alongside Indonesian Air Force EMB-314 Super Tucano aircraft, Bell-412 helicopters and Joint Terminal Attack Controllers.

The following is the Oct. 22, 2026, Congressional Research Service report, The U.S. Army’s Infantry Squad Vehicle (ISV).

From the Report

The ISV is a lightweight, unarmored ground transport vehicle being developed by GM Defense (headquartered in Detroit, MI) intended to enhance the mobility of Army Mobile Brigade Combat Teams (MBCTs), Security Force Assistance Brigades (SFABs), and Army Special Operations Forces. According to the Army, the ISV was designed to move nine soldiers and their equipment rapidly across terrain where heavier vehicles such as the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV) or High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle (HMMWV) may be less practical or effective.

The JLTV, HMMWV, and ISV constitute the Army’s Light Tactical Vehicle (LTV) fleet. The Army has evaluated the ISV as part of the Army’s Transformation in Contact (TIC) modernization program. Previous reliance on HMMWVs and JLTVs, which offered greater protection, reportedly presented challenges in terms of speed, cross-country mobility, and air transport. The Army adopted a commercial off‑the‑shelf (COTS) acquisition approach for the ISV to minimize costs and field the vehicle quickly. GM Defense’s Chevrolet Colorado ZR2 mid-sized truck was chosen as the baseline ISV platform, deriving 90 percent of its parts from COTS components, with modifications made for suspension, structure, and load‑carrying capacity.

item.content:encoded:
MANILA, Philippines — A U.S. Marine Corps drone detachment is operating from a Philippine airfield in Palawan near South China Sea flashpoints in the Spratly Islands, USNI News has learned. 

From the airfield, Washington can potentially support Manila with more intensive intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions of Chinese forces operating off the Philippines. 

Marine Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Squadron 1 (VMU-1) is operating out of Antonio Bautista Air Base, according to a logistics document reviewed by USNI News. An expeditionary hangar recently appeared on commercial open source satellite imagery posted on Apple Maps. The hangar is the same make of one currently in use by VMU-1 at Basa Air Base in Luzon. 

Located at Palawan’s provincial capital of Puerto Princesa, the unit’s MQ-9A Reapers can sortie for missions over maritime features more than 300 miles away. The drones’ onboard sensors can also monitor China’s expansive military deployments off the Philippines, which includes several artificial island bases. The drones are further evidence of Washington’s tactical presence during incidents between Chinese and Philippine forces. 

“Flying from Puerto Princesa rather than Basa Air Base on Luzon cuts a Reaper’s transit to Second Thomas Shoal from more than 400 nautical miles to under 200. That’s nearly three extra hours over the target on every sortie,” Ben Lewis, founder of PLA Tracker, an organization dedicated to monitoring Chinese military activity and development, told USNI News. 

The Philippine Air Force base is one of nine designated under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement for Washington to stage equipment and deploy troops on a rotational basis. 

VMU-1’s Palawan detachment is also adjacent to the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ Western Command headquarters. This command directly oversees Philippine operations in the contested Spratly Islands, including resupply missions to BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57) at Second Thomas Shoal. 

The detachment can support MQ-9As for South China Sea sorties from an additional site outside of Luzon, which is prone to weather disruptions via typhoons, according to Lewis. 

“Incidents can escalate within hours, so a persistent picture of what is moving and where gives Manila and Washington earlier warning and a firmer evidential basis for responding,” said Lewis.

The detachment at Puerto Princesa expands American drone deployments across the Philippines. VMU-1’s drones began deploying to the Philippines in 2024 following a request from Manila to assist its South China Sea intelligence gathering efforts. 

Army drones have been deployed for over a decade on the southern island of Mindanao for counter-insurgency support. However, these drones have also been seen shadowing maritime incidents at contested maritime features. 

The Marine Corps acknowledged but did not return requests for information on the VMU-1 detachment at Puerto Princesa. In September, USNI News inquired about the reason for the deployment to Palawan and the beginning of its mission at Antonio Bautista. 

The VMU-1 deployment coincides with an increased tempo of American defense drills and investments across the Southeast Asian archipelago.

Washington’s efforts in expanding military infrastructure and rotational deployments to Manila are occurring as China consolidates its South China Sea claims. Military construction efforts at EDCA sites are increasing the capacity for rotational forces and forward-deployed equipment. A non-stop season of Spring and early Summer exercises effectively deploys thousands of U.S. troops to the Philippines annually. 

Tensions between Beijing and Manila have spiraled in recent years, at times resulting in incidents involving rammings, water cannons and clashes at various shoals. 

“With Coast Guard cutters rotating through Subic in September and now Marines positioning in Palawan, Washington is sending a signal that we stand with the Philippines in the South China Sea,” Ryan Claffey, a Research Assistant with the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Center for a New American Security, told USNI News.

According to Claffey, the specifics of these deployments may be kept quiet to prevent tensions ahead of international engagements with China, such as APEC and the G20. Going forward, Claffey said he expects more U.S. intelligence sharing, joint patrols and long-range missile deployments to the Philippines.

The U.S. Marine Corps recently used the Neros Archer First Person View drone in a live-fire exercise at Camp Fuji, Japan, for the first time, the service announced. 

Marines of Battalion Landing Team 1/1, 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU) carried out two strike missions on Oct. 20 at Combined Arms Training Center, Camp Fuji with the Neros Archer based on two different scenarios as a proof of concept tied to the unit’s hunter-killer teams. 

Neros Archer is the current Marine Corps’ program of record for one-way attack drones flown by a first-person view pilot. The Marine Corps issued a contract in November of 2025 to Neros for an unspecified number of Neros Archer drones to be deployed across the Fleet Marine Force. 

The hunter-killer concept for drones sees an Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) drone detecting and tracking targets, passing coordinates to a paired FPV strike-drone operator who executes a precision kinetic strike. The exercises this month were meant to extend the Marines’ capabilities with defeating armor and interdicting ground line communications of adversaries, according to a service news release. 

One flight scenario was designed as an anti-armor ambush. CATC Camp Fuji Explosive Ordnance technicians also attended the drone test as the drones were equipped with explosive payloads. Both scenarios involved successful detonations of the targets, the service said. 

A few dozen observers watched the exercise as the Marines flew the drone for two separate flights on Oct. 20. Imagery released of the exercise show that members of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force observed the drills. 

Neros Archer drones are operated by junior enlisted Marines between the ranks of lance corporal to sergeant with unit leadership hand-picking a Marine to take part in the three-week training course. No prior drone experience is the only pre-requisite for selection as with nothing to compare to, it ensures that the operator can master the skills needed for the Neros Archer drone, the service announcement reads.

“All this is handled by non-commissioned officers and non-NCOs,” said Master Sgt. Glenn Dayton, Company Operations Chief, Weapons Company, Battalion Landing Team 1/1, 31st MEU. “You’re looking at the heart and soul of our ground force. This is not executed by staff NCO or officers, I think that’s a huge aspect. Our lower enlisted are the ones we rely on to master this craft.”

Japan-based U.S. Marines have also been experimenting with deploying Neros Archer from maritime platforms to carry out reconnaissance missions at the shore. A Pentagon imagery release shows a Marine of 3rd Battalion 7th Marine Regiment, forward deployed with 4th Marine Regiment, 3rd Marine Division, as part of the Unit Deployment Program, launching a Neros Archer drone from a Multi-Mission Reconnaissance Craft-B off the coast of Okinawa on Sept. 18. 

“The training served as a proof of concept for employing small unmanned aircraft systems from maritime platforms in support of sea-to-shore operations,” reads the image caption.

Late last month, the drone was used in the U.S. National Drone Association Drone Crucible 26.3 exercise and competition held Sept. 27 to Oct. 2 in Starke, Fla. 

“In an evolving battlefield the Marines of 2nd [Marine Division] are using exercises such as the Drone Crucible to refine their skills, combat these developing threats and maintain the legacy as the tip of the spear,” reads a Marine Corps news release.

The USNDA-hosted exercise is primarily focused on modernizing squad-level capabilities in the use of drones and counter-drone technologies and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTP) and also works to enhance squad level capabilities through employment and evaluation of short-term future systems, according to a USNDA description of the exercise.

The 2nd Marine Division conducted approximately 140 Small Unmanned Aerial Systems (SUAS) flights during Drone Crucible to assess system durability, develop new standard operating procedures and build pilot proficiency under various flight conditions, including in low light. 

“The fight doesn’t stop just because the sun goes down,” said 2nd Lt. Tanner Wodovick, a platoon commander with 2nd Battalion, 2nd Marine Regiment, 2nd MARDIV.“It’s a new experience for the pilot, so we’re getting them used to it.”

Low-light operations added another layer of complexity for the drone team, reads the 2nd Marine Division release. 

For the competition, pilots used thermal cameras to positively identify targets before striking. The team developed hand and arm signals to reduce noise signatures at night. The training helped operators become familiar with night-flight procedures and use their systems effectively in low-light conditions, the service said. 

“We’re testing out new thermal cameras for the drones. Being able to fly at night is a new capability of ours, as well as doing night strikes and flying inside buildings with these drones.” said Sgt. Xander Morris, a drone operator with 2nd Battalion, 2nd Marine Regiment, 2nd MARDIV.

Drone Crucible is designed to enable flexible field experimentation and a key part of that experimentation was testing hunter-killer integration at the small-unit level, giving drone teams a chance to develop standard operating procedures in complex urban environments, including long-distance navigation and operations within structures. 

“We can strike a target with precision and also have the capability to have an ISR platform up in the air to be able to give us corrections, spotting and do long-range strikes beyond line-of-sight strikes,” said Morris. “It’s really good training and whatever tactics we see fit, we can try out here.”

item.content:encoded:
The Navy saw the most Class A aviation and afloat mishaps in at least in a decade, according to Fiscal Year 2026 data recently released by the Navy Safety Command. 

The Navy had 16 aviation Class A mishaps, which include manned and unmanned flights, as well as ground aviation, between Oct. 1, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026. A Class A mishap is defined by the Naval Safety Command as one that causes at least $2.5 million in damage and/or aircraft to be destroyed. A permanent disability or fatality would also put a mishap in the Class A category. 

Sixteen aviation mishaps is the most the Navy has had since Fiscal Year 2014, when the Navy had 17. 

The 16 aviation mishaps include an incident on Oct. 26, 2025, when an F/A18F Super Hornet and an MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter crashed into the South China Sea in two separate occurrences. Both aircraft were assigned to USS Nimitz (CVN-68) at the time of the crashes.

The data also include two separate Growler crashes – one on May 17 and one on Sept. 28. The May incident saw two EA-18G Growlers crash during an airshow, with all four aviators ejecting. The one on Sept. 28 left four sailors injured after a landing mishap aboard USS Dwight D. Eisenhower (CVN-69).

The data also include the death of an aviator after their MH-60S helicopter, assigned to USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77), ditched into the Arabian Sea. 

Of the 16 aviation mishaps, two involved unmanned aircraft. Of the 14 manned aircraft incidents, 11 were flight mishaps, while three were ground mishaps. 

The Navy also saw 11 afloat mishaps in FY 2026, the highest since at least 2014. 

The incidents include the presumed death of Lance Cpl. Chukwuemeka Oforah, who fell overboard from USS Iwo Jima (LHD-7) on Feb. 7, and the death of Lance Cpl. Armando Ortiz Canseco, attached to San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS Anchorage (LPD-23), who went missing at-sea on June 25. 

The 11 also included the collision between guided-missile destroyer USS Truxtun (DDG-103) and fast oiler USNS Supply (AOE-6) on Feb. 11.

There were also two fires – the April 19 fire aboard USS Zumwalt (DDG-1000) at HII Ingalls Shipbuilding, which injured three people, and the March 12 fire aboard USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78), which injured at least two sailors. 

While the Navy saw the most aviation and afloat mishaps in at least 10 fiscal years, it did not see the same for total on-duty Class A mishaps. In FY 2026, the Navy had 30 total on-duty Class A mishaps – the most since 2022 when the sea service also had 30. 

However, between FY 2024-26, the Navy typically saw a total number of on-duty Class A mishaps in the 20s, with only three years — fiscal years 2014, 2022 and 2026 – having at least 30 mishaps. 

The two other on-duty fatalities in FY 2026 include a 46-year-old lieutenant commander who died after a motorcycle crash during a military motorcycle safety group ride and a death during physical training. 

The Navy saw 48 off-duty mishaps, which resulted in 45 fatalities. That was down from the previous year, which had 54 mishaps and 53 fatalities. 

The Marine Corps had six aviation mishaps in FY 2026, up one from FY 2025. Of the six, five were flight mishaps and one was a ground mishap. 

The five included the Oct. 16 AH-1Z Viper attack helicopter crash in southern California that killed Maj. Tyler Braconi.

The service also had five ground on-duty mishaps, which included one tactical vehicle mishap. 

Physical training fatalities rose by one, with five in FY 2026 compared to four in FY 2025. 

Overall, the Marine Corps had 12 on-duty mishaps with seven fatalities. Four of the deaths occurred during or from physical training. 

The Marine Corps had 24 off-duty Class A mishaps with 24 off-duty fatalities in FY 2026, down from 36 mishaps and 34 fatalities in FY 2025.

Five are dead after U.S. forces struck a suspected narco boat in the Eastern Pacific, U.S. Southern Command announced on Tuesday.
“On Oct. 27, under the direction of #SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific,” reads a statement on X.

According to SOUTHCOM, unspecified intelligence indicated those operating the boat were trafficking drugs and referred to the individuals killed as “narco-terrorists.”

A total of 243 people have been killed as part of the Southern Command strikes, based on USNI News tabulation.

While the Trump administration has touted the strikes as lowering fatal overdoses in the country, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data do not show a noticeable decrease in overdoses since President Donald Trump announced the first strike in September of 2025. Overall, overdoses in the U.S. have decreased since September of 2023.

Fentanyl, which the Trump administration has said is in the alleged drug boats, typically comes into the U.S. through the U.S.-Mexico border via passenger vehicles, while supplies often come from China, according to Government Accountability Office reports.

Last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. would work with regional allies as the “most effective” way to take on trafficking, according to The Associated Press.

item.content:encoded:
Marine Rotational Force-Darwin 26.3 completed its six month rotational deployment to Australia and the Indo-Pacific, the service announced on Friday. 

The conclusion of the MRF-D’s deployment marks the 15th rotation, reads a Marine Corps news release. During the deployment, the rotational force was certified as a Special Purpose Marine Air-Ground Task Force – the first time a MRF-D has received the special certification.

The MRF-D, led by 5th Marine Regiment, 1st Marine Division, combined 2,000 Marines and sailors from I and III Marine Expeditionary forces into a force capable of bringing together command and control, aviation, ground combat and logistics capabilities, reads the release. The rotational force trained alongside the Australian Defence Force and regional allies and partners from March to October throughout Australia, the Philippines, New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, French Polynesia and Indonesia. 

As a certified Special Purpose Marine Air-Ground Task Force, the MRF-D acted as a forward-postured stand-in force in the region and was capable of operating from dispersed locations and responding quickly to crises.

“This 15th rotation stands as a testament to what the U.S. and Australia can achieve when we train shoulder-to-shoulder,” U.S. Marine Corps Col. George Flynn, commanding officer of MRF-D 26.3 SPMAGT, said in the release. “I want to extend my deepest gratitude to our ADF counterparts and our hosts across the country for their unwavering support. By pushing our limits together during exercises like Render Safe, Predators Run, Southern Jackaroo and Capital Reach, we have learned immensely from one another. We have forged an unparalleled level of interoperability, proving that we can move together rapidly and effectively to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

Preparations for the deployment began in the U.S. before the unit arrived in Australia with participation in Exercise Steel Knight 2025. Conducted across Southern California from Dec. 1-14, 2025, the still-forming force established geographically distributed command-and-control nodes and rehearsed long-distance movement of personnel and equipment using MV-22B Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and C-130J Super Hercules aircraft. 

Marines and sailors also underwent evaluations on their ability to conduct embassy reinforcement, evacuation operations, casualty evacuation, expeditionary medical support, aviation-node operations and expeditionary advanced base operations.

Following its arrival in Darwin, MRF-D 26.3 began its regional training campaign with Exercise Balikatan 2026, held from April 20 to May 8 in the Philippines. The exercise provided the final operational environment for MRF-D 26.3 to complete its SPMAGTF certification. During Balikatan, Marines and sailors validated their ability to recover aircraft and personnel, conduct aviation external lift, deliver supplies by air to a notional civilian population and establish expeditionary advanced bases in austere, dispersed locations.

In Aporawan, Palawan, as part of Balikatan, MRF-D’s ground combat element trained alongside the Armed Forces of the Philippines, Australian Defense Force, New Zealand Defense Force and U.S. joint forces during a counter-landing live-fire exercise. The combined force synchronized Philippine Marine Corps artillery, High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, mortars, crew-served weapons, anti-armor systems and air-defense capabilities against simulated amphibious threats.

Balikatan culminated on May 3 at Balabac Island, where multinational reconnaissance teams from the Philippine Marine Corps, Australian Army and 1st Reconnaissance Battalion shaped the operational environment before U.S., Philippine and Australian forces conducted an air assault to secure Balabac Airfield. Marine Medium Tiltrotor Squadron 268 (Reinforced) transported personnel and equipment from Antonio Bautista Air Base, while U.S. Army watercraft moved HIMARS into the austere maritime environment. The combined force then integrated air mobility, reconnaissance, ground maneuver and fires during a live-fire demonstration against simulated maritime targets.

Coinciding with Balikatan, elements of the force deployed to New Caledonia for Exercise Tagata Toa, a multinational combined-arms exercise hosted by the French Armed Forces from April 27 to May 10. The deployment to New Caledonia also demonstrated the importance of partner-enabled mobility, reads the release. The Royal New Zealand Air Force provided a Boeing 757 and two C-130 Hercules aircraft to move Marines and equipment between Darwin, New Caledonia and Townsville. 

“By drawing on allied capacity, access and professional relationships, MRF-D moved personnel and equipment across international boundaries faster than it could have through unilateral means. That ability to leverage partner capabilities expanded the combined force’s reach and resilience across the Indo-Pacific,” reads the release.

The special purpose MAGTF then returned its focus to northern Australia on May 18 with Exercise Predators Walk, which continued through June 12 and built tactical familiarity between Marines and Australian counterparts. 

Then, from May 29 to July 3 in Townsville, Marines trained alongside Australian and Japanese forces during Exercise Southern Jackaroo. The exercise included joint operations and live-fire training designed to strengthen combined readiness and interoperability in complex terrain. Other elements of the units deployed to the Philippines for Exercise KAMANDAG 10, held June 15 to July 1.

The MRF-D then participated in a month-long deployment as part of participation in Operation Render Safe, the multinational effort to remove World War II-era unexploded ordnance and reduce risks to communities in East New Britain. From July 1-31, Marines of the MRF-D 26.3 explosive ordnance disposal element disposed of 732 munitions totalling 16,041 pounds of net explosive weight.

From July 20 to Aug. 7, MRF-D 26 joined the Australian Army’s 1st Brigade and the Philippine Army’s 1st Brigade Combat Team for Exercise Predators Run 26, in the Townsville Field Training Area. The trilateral exercise integrated U.S., Australian and Philippine forces under a unified command structure for platoon-level training, force-on-force maneuvers and a combined defensive live-fire scenario. The unit employed multiple organic unmanned aircraft systems to expand logistics, medical support and ground-combat capabilities during the exercise

An embarked deployment took place in early August with Royal Australian Navy amphibious assault ship HMAS Canberra (L02). VMM-268 (Rein.) conducted MV-22B Osprey deck landing qualifications, while the Royal Australian Navy mechanized landing craft transported Marine Corps Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTV) and Medium Tactical Vehicle Replacements from Canberra’s well deck to shore.

In Indonesia from Aug. 12-28, Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, 5th Marines conducted an annual platoon exchange with Indonesian marines from 7th Infantry Battalion, 4th Brigade near Lampung. Then, from Aug. 31 toSept.11, 230 Marines and sailors joined Indonesian and multinational partners for combined-arms live fire, jungle operations, small-unit tactics, force-on-force training and subject-matter expert exchange as part of Exercise Super Garuda Shield 2026.

The rotational force is scheduled to return to the Northern Territory in early 2027 for the 16th MRF-D rotation, according to an Australian Defense Department news release. 

I MEF deploys two rotational forces to the Indo-Pacific – MRF-D and Marine Rotational Force-South East Asia (MRF-SEA). In previous years, MRF-SEA would deploy from October to March with MRF-D entering the region in April. However, since April this year, MRF-SEA has maintained its command element on a continuous basis in the Philippines with the unit’s recent activity being a bilateral planning exercise with Philippine Joint Task Force personnel from Oct. 5-9.

“For MRF-SEA, the planning exercise represents the progression of a rotation built around persistent engagement with Philippine partners,” reads a MRF-SEA news release.
