The following is the full English translation of Japan’s 2026 Defense White Paper, released Oct. 26, 2026.

From the Report

Security Environment Surrounding Japan Overview

International Community amid the Greatest Trial of the Postwar Era

States that do not share universal values or political and economic systems based on such values are expanding their influence. Unilateral changes to the status quo by force and such attempts represent a serious challenge to the existing international order. The international community is facing its greatest trial since World War II and entering a new era of crisis. The global balance of power is shifting dramatically and competition among states is growing. In particular, the inter-state competition between the U.S. and China is likely to intensify even further in the future.

Rapid developments in science and technology are fundamentally changing the paradigm of security. Countries are striving to develop innovative technologies that can become so-called game changers. The traditional military structure is undergoing fundamental changes, as are warfare tactics and strategies.

Risks in cyberspace and other domains are becoming more serious, and other security-related global issues such as information warfare and climate change are emerging.

Gray zone situations involving territorial disputes are constantly occurring. The use of hybrid warfare, which combines military and non-military means, may become even more sophisticated.
Increasingly Severe Security Situation in the Indo-Pacific Region

Such global security environment and challenges are particularly prominent in the Indo-Pacific region, where Japan is located, and are likely to intensify still further in the future.

It cannot be ruled out that a serious situation similar to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine may occur in the Indo-Pacific region in the future, particularly in East Asia.

Russia’s Aggression and Ukraine’s Defense

Russia’s aggression against Ukraine undermines the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. It is a serious violation of international law prohibiting the use of force and of the United Nations (UN) Charter. Such unilateral changes to the status quo by force have shaken the very foundation of the international order, including in Asia.

This situation, in which a permanent member of the Security Council, which is supposed to take primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, openly engages in military actions challenging international law and the international order, claims innocent lives and repeatedly uses language and actions that can be interpreted as threats involving nuclear weapons, is unprecedented.

If such aggression is tolerated, it could send out the wrong message and implication that unilateral changes to the status quo by force are also acceptable elsewhere.

Accordingly, the international community, including Japan, should not tolerate Russia’s action.

In addition to Ukraine’s strong resistance, the international community has united to implement strong sanctions and other measures. As an ally of the U.S.—a NATO member—and a country located on the opposite side of Europe across the Eurasian continent, Japan must closely monitor future changes in the European situation, including their strategic impact, acknowledging that the security of Europe and the Indo-Pacific is inseparable.

Defense Policies of Other Countries and Regions

The U.S. – Security Policy and Activities of the Second Trump Administration

The second Trump administration was formed in January 2025. The National Security Strategy was released in December of the same year, followed by the National Defense Strategy in January 2026. These documents clarified the security strategy envisioned by the second Trump administration.

Under the banner of “America First,” the Department of War indicated its intention to restore “peace through strength” and to focus on the Indo-Pacific region, where Japan is located, while prioritizing homeland defense. The documents also provide detailed descriptions of relations with allies, among other matters.

China – Intensified Unilateral Attempts and Activities to Change the Status Quo by Force or Coercion

China’s external posture, military activities, and other activities are a matter of serious concern for Japan and the international community and present an unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge which Japan should respond with its comprehensive national power and in cooperation and collaboration with its ally, like-minded countries, and others.

For more than 30 years, China has sustained high-level growth of its defense budget without transparency, engaging in broad and rapid improvement of its military power in qualitative and quantitative terms with a focus on nuclear, missile, naval, and air forces.

China has been intensifying its activities in the region surrounding Japan, including the East China Sea, particularly in the area around the Senkaku Islands, the Sea of Japan, and the western Pacific Ocean, extending beyond the so-called first island chain to the second island chain.

In 2025, a series of incidents occurred, including: the activity of an aircraft carrier in the waters east of Iwo-To and the activity of two aircraft carriers in the Pacific Ocean in June; the unusual close approach by a Chinese fighter aircraft to a Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) aircraft in June; the unusual close approach by a Chinese fighter-bomber to a JSDF aircraft in July; the activity of an aircraft carrier in the Pacific Ocean from the east of the main island of Okinawa to the east of Amami Oshima Island in December; and intermittent radar illumination against a JSDF aircraft by a Chinese fighter for approximately 30 minutes in December.

Such unusual close approaches by Chinese military aircraft could have triggered an accidental collision. Furthermore, the radar illumination by the Chinese military aircraft was a dangerous act exceeding the range necessary for the safe flight of an aircraft, and it is extremely regrettable that such incidents took place.

China has intensified its military activities around Taiwan. China conducted military exercises in the sea and airspace several times. It is believed that through the series of activities, China seeks to create a fait accompli where the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is operating, and improve its actual combat capabilities.

China has intensified its activities in the South China Sea, while promoting militarization, based on assertions of unlawful maritime claims. Such actions to further promote its attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are serious concerns to Japan. Issues surrounding the South China Sea are directly connected to peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region and represent a legitimate concern, not only for Japan, which has major sea lanes in the South China Sea, but also for the entire international community.

China is further strengthening its cooperation with Russia, including in military activities. In the Commemoration of the 80th Anniversary of the Victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War in September 2025, President Xi Jinping, President Vladimir Putin, and Chairman of the State Affairs Commission Kim Jong Un were seen standing side by side. In the vicinity of Japan, China and Russia conducted joint flights of bombers and joint navigations of vessels. Such repeated joint activities are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and pose a grave concern for Japan’s security.

This post has been updated to include that USS Colorado (SSN-788) arrived in Australia on Oct. 26.

The Pentagon announced Monday the Virginia-class submarine that will be the lead nuclear attack boat in western Australia.

USS Colorado (SSN-788) will be assigned to Submarine Rotational Force-West, which will be based HMAS Stirling outside of Perth starting in 2027.

“The selection of USS Colorado as the first submarine assigned to SRF-West in 2027 marks a significant milestone for AUKUS Pillar I and is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific,” reads a Monday statement from the Australian Government and Pentagon leadership.

Following an earlier version of this post, the Navy announced Colorado had arrived in Stirling for a maintenance period.

The deployment of Colorado is one of the early steps of the AUKUS Pillar I agreement between the U.S., U.K. and Australia to build the infrastructure for Australia to field three to five Virginia-class attack boats for the Royal Australian Navy in the 2030s.

Under current plans, SRF-West will eventually host four Virginia-class submarines and a U.K. nuclear attack boat as part of the AUKUS construct.

The announcement comes ahead of the third annual maintenance period of an American Virginia-class boat in Stirling as part of preparing for the rotational deployments. In 2024, USS Hawaii (SSN-776) pulled was repaired by a crew aboard the submarine tender USS Emory S. Land (AS-39). Last year, USS Vermont (SSN-792) arrived in Stirling for an availability with Australian workers without the tender.

Royal Navy nuclear attack submarine HMS Anson (S123) arrived in February for its own availability with the Australian maintenance teams.

Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility has been tasked with training Australian workers to repair Virginias as well as overseeing a repair and logistics attachment at Stirling. The public yard completed its maintenance period earlier this year.

The U.S. Navy established two commands earlier this year to support the effort — Naval Support Activity (NSA) Stirling and Submarine Squadron 3.

“With SRF-West, we have submarines rotating through a critical region with an organic, predominately Australian, maintenance workforce keeping those boats fit to fight. That not only supports readiness, but it also reduces the burden on the U.S. shipyards and increases our fast-attack submarine force’s readiness while preparing Australia to maintain their own SSNs,” reads a June statement from Director of Submarine Programs Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher.

In a Monday statement on the announcement, Rep Joe Courtney (D-Conn.) praised the move.

“The combination of U.S. and U.K. attack submarine rotations and Australian nuclear-powered submarines will transform allied naval posture in the Indo-Pacific. AUKUS Pillars I and II continue full steam ahead with Congress and the Navy in lock step with the U.K. and Australia,” he said in a statement.

The Royal Navy currently lacks the ships and capabilities needed to defend the High North from Russia, the bipartisan House of Commons Defense Committee warned on Thursday. 

In its “Defense in the High North” report issued on Thursday, the committee described the Royal Navy as being plagued by shipbuilding delays, maintenance backlogs and an atrophying submarine force.

“The U.K. needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the U.K., including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defense has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the U.K. can meet its commitments in the High North,” said Tan Dhesi, chair of the defense committee and a Labor Party member of Parliament.

The report put 2030 as the deadline for the U.K. to be militarily ready to deter or defeat a Russian threat, citing then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s statement in June that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030, according to an assessment by the U.K. and allied intelligence services.

“If the U.K. government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough,” Dhesi said.

The U.K. Defense Investment Plan released in June committed to investing £298 billion – $397.9 billion – across the next four years to reach 2.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) spent on defense by 2030. The committee noted an internal document drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises. The U.K. was at number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries, according to the committee report. 

“Only Iceland, a country with no military capability, is lower on the table,” reads the committee report.

The Royal Navy’s anti-submarine warfare frigates and nuclear-powered submarines offer the greatest deterrent to Russian activities in the High North, however both are aging or unavailable due to maintenance issues. Additionally, the Royal Navy established in 2010 a requirement for a fleet of six destroyers and 13 frigates but has struggled to meet this requirement. The current fleet consists of six Type 45 destroyers and five Type 23 frigates – barely half of the requirement for a 19 ship fleet.

“Although new frigates will eventually join the fleet in sufficient numbers, the current fleet readiness picture raises doubts about whether the U.K. could sustain the maritime tasks required in the High North by 2030,” reads the report.

Particularly critical to the capabilities needed in the High North is the requirement for eight of the 13 frigates to be fitted with the Sonar 2087 towed array to undertake anti-submarine warfare operations. The towed array is currently on all the remaining five Type 23s. 

The slow construction and delivery of the Type 26s has led to a capability gap in the Royal Navy’s ASW frigate numbers. The first-in-class Type 26 was laid down in 2017 and is scheduled to be accepted in 2027. Eight Type 26 frigates will take over the ASW role in the future with five Type 31 general purpose ships making up the remaining frigate requirement.

The ASW frigates could be as low as five for the next three years, according to the committee. Two of the under construction Royal Navy Type 26s will be sold to meet Norway’s 2025 order – to be in service by 2039 – which means the Royal Navy won’t meet its eight ASW frigate requirement until 2037. 

The Defense Committee recommended that no more Type 23s should leave service until they are replaced on a one-for-one basis by the Type 26.

The Royal Navy has also faced challenges in maintaining its destroyers, aircraft carriers, amphibious ships and submarines, all of which can provide military capabilities useful for High North operations, the Defense Committee said. 

Both the Royal Navy’s Queen Elizabeth-class carriers broke down in 2022 and 2024 due to propeller shaft issues. The Royal Navy’s two specialist amphibious assault ships were decommissioned in November of 2024 ahead of their planned inactivation dates of 2033 and 2034. The U.K. and the Netherlands have since signed a contract to procure a fleet of four amphibious vessels each, but these are unlikely to be in service until the 2030s.

Destroyer HMS Dragon (D35) was pulled out of maintenance in March to deploy to Cyprus to defend against drone attacks.

“The fact that no other destroyer was ready to deploy from the fleet of Type 45 vessels may reflect the lack of deployable ships. As these platforms provide air defense, they would be equally important in any High North operation,” said the Defense Committee.

In addition, all five Astute-class nuclear attack submarines were all recently tied up in dockyards at the same time, with none deployed. The Defense Committee also pointed to the atrophying of the Royal Navy’s submarine capability and questioned its ability to operate under the ice. 

“Without a credible under-ice capability, the U.K. is less able to contest Russian freedom of action in the High North and risks being forced into a more defensive posture. Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines, while threatening NATO sea lanes, U.K. critical infrastructure and the nuclear deterrent,” said the Defense Committee.

The report recommended that the government provide the Defense Committee with a plan outlining how the Ministry of Defense will improve the availability of the Royal Navy’s frigates, destroyers and attack submarines before 2030. This update may be presented at a classified level, but the committee will expect a version to be publicly available. 

The Defense Committee report calls for the government to brief its progress to re-establish an under-ice capability for at least some of the Astute-class submarines.

Regarding the U.K.’s Hybrid Navy program, the committee said it is not convinced that the £1.3 billion – or $1.7 billion USD – allocated for the program will be sufficient. While the committee encourages the pursuit of naval exports, it said the government needs to ensure that the exports did not compete with the U.K.’s own requirements for scarce ships, systems and skilled labor.

The allocated funds cover the procurement of five vessel types – the Type 91 uncrewed missile platform, Type 92 uncrewed sloop with underwater sensors, Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels (XLUUVs), Type 94 uncrewed radar platforms and a future class of crewed Common Combat Vessels (CCV). The report calls on the government to set out the basis on which it judges the current funding allocation to be adequate.

The Defense Committee said that defense exports can strengthen the U.K.’s position in the High North when they help closely aligned allies field capabilities that are interoperable with the Royal Navy and are suited to northern operations. The Type 26 agreement with Norway could expand NATO’s ASW capacity on the northern flank and deepen U.K.-Norwegian operational and industrial integration. However, the report said export success must not come at the expense of the Royal Navy’s own Type 26 frigate delivery timelines.

“The government must ensure that naval exports expand industrial capacity and allied capability, rather than competing with U.K. requirements for scarce ships, systems and skilled labor,” reads the Defense Committee report.

In contrast, the committee said the Royal Marines capabilities for High North operations were excellent, due to its expertise from regular deployments to Northern Norway, logistic capabilities and the Commando Helicopter Force. However, the Royal Marines can’t compensate for the naval platforms’ shortfalls.

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard’s new patrol vessel from Taiwan shadowed the Chinese Navy’s Liaoning Carrier Strike Group on Friday off Mindanao. 

BRP Sarangani (6177) shadowed the 60,000-ton Chinese aircraft carrier Liaoning (16) and its guided-missile destroyer escorts Anshan (101), Wuxi (104) and Huainan (123) in the Basilan Strait, local media outlet Bilyonaryo News Channel reported Saturday. Philippine Navy frigate BRP Diego Silang (FFG-7) and patrol vessel BRP Emilio Jacinto (PS-35) also observed the Liaoning CSG, according to the report. 

The escort is the first publicized tasking for the ex-Taiwan Coast Guard Administration vessel Kinmen (123) – now Sarangani – in Philippine service. Transferred through the We Protect our Seas Foundation last month, Manila’s maritime security agency took possession of the vessel under the condition that it would not be used near or against Taiwan. During the vessel’s commissioning on Oct. 2, the PCG said that Sarangani would be stationed in Mindanao. 

The People’s Liberation Army Navy strike group officially began training activities across the Western Pacific earlier this month in the East China Sea. Since Oct. 14, the Liaoning CSG has sailed around the Japanese Ryukyu Islands, into the Philippine Sea, through the Luzon Strait and into the South China Sea. Within the last two weeks, the Liaoning CSG’s voyage has seen three First Island Chain transits. 

In recent years, the PLAN has increasingly used Philippine archipelagic waters in the Sulu Sea and Southern Mindanao to transit the First Island Chain. Chinese aircraft carriers and spy ships have used the route to access the Philippine Sea for training activities and operations around Australia. 

While the region hosts the bulk of the Armed Forces of the Philippines active forces, Manila’s posture in Mindanao is focused against internal security threats such as piracy and counter-insurgency. The recent appearance of Chinese warships and cutters has fueled the deployment of new units to face conventional threats in the southern waters. 

Compared to the traditional maritime chokepoints between the Northern Philippines, Taiwan and Southern Japan, the waters around Mindanao can offer another less observed route into the open waters of the Pacific, according to Ben Lewis, founder of PLA Tracker, an organization dedicated to monitoring Chinese military activity and development. 

“The Luzon Strait is heavily watched by Taiwan, the Philippines, Japan and the U.S. The Sulu Sea is much less so, which gives the PLAN another way into the Pacific and gets its crews familiar with it,” Lewis told USNI News.

Guided-missile destroyer USS McFaul (DDG-74) returned Friday to Naval Station Norfolk, Va., after 11 months deployed.

McFaul left Norfolk on Nov. 25, 2026, for an independent deployment and spent the bulk of the time away in the Middle East.

“The sailors of USS McFaul have performed exceptionally well during this demanding combat deployment, proving themselves as a true warfighting powerhouse. Operating in a highly volatile region, this crew has repeatedly demonstrated the grit, technical mastery and resilience required to protect our strike group and execute complex missions under pressure,” McFaul’s commander Cmdr. Adam Samson said in a statement. “I could not be more proud of their unwavering dedication and the quiet professionalism they bring to the watch every single day.”

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and U.S. Fleet Forces commander Adm. Karl Thomas were on hand to see the crew of the destroyer return to the naval base on Friday, according to photos released by the service.

According to USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker, McFaul sailed through the Mediterranean Sea, to the Red Sea, through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and spent the majority of its deployment supporting the naval build up in the North Arabian Sea.

“The warship provided anti-air warfare, surface warfare and naval surface fire support during combat operations, integrating with the USS Abraham Lincoln, USS George H.W. Bush, and USS George Washington carrier strike groups,” reads the Friday statement.

McFaul returned by circumnavigating Africa rather than returning via the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. The U.S. Navy has largely avoided sailing through the maritime chokepoint of the Bab el-Mandeb that links the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden due to its proximity to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, USNI News understands. USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77) arrived in the region on the same route earlier this year.

McFaul and West Coast-based USS Spruance (DDG-111), which deployed in November with USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), were two of the longest-serving destroyers as part of the naval operations in the Middle East. U.S. destroyers have been in on and off combat operations since shortly after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack in Southern Israel in response to Houthi threats to maritime shipping.

Now the Navy has more than a dozen destroyers supporting the naval blockade in U.S. 5th Fleet.

The demand on the Navy’s versatile multi-mission warships are reshaping how the Navy deploys and trains its force, leaders said last month.

“The traditional model of naval ship maintenance is no longer viable in this high-demand operational environment,” Fleet Forces commander Thomas said at a maintenance conference. “That’s what we [have] got to change.”

On Thursday, Defense One reported families of destroyer sailors could expect deployments of a year or longer.

This post has been updated to include photos from the AUKUS Pillar II “Maritime Big Play-Pacific” demonstration in Southern California. 

SAN DIEGO, Calif. — At first glance, the Hadalus-XL unmanned underwater vehicle and its dark flat panels might not catch the curious eye like a go-fast boat or sleek fighter jet.

But its value is in what it does, said Ben Rosenthal, chief technology officer with Composite Energy Technologies, a Rhode Island-based company. The 34-foot underwater vehicle can haul several tons of cargo. Its panels and components fold flat for transport in a 20-foot container, packaged for quick assembly or disassembly with simple tools. 

“We’re kind of a pickup truck of the ocean. We can bring big, heavy things into position,” Rosenthal told USNI News on Wednesday while standing next to the extra-large, UUV variant parked on a submarine pier at Naval Base Point Loma. “It’s much bigger and much heavier than any other vehicle that’s out there.”

Hadalus-XL might not be the sexiest tech, but the utility of such an autonomous vehicle is meant to be clear to maritime commanders needing to resupply forces, track an enemy submarine, counter-attack or call for fire support.

“What wins wars is logistics,” Rosenthal said.

Logistics is among the growing threats U.S. military officials are focused on through the trilateral AUKUS security agreement between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The proliferation of cheap, high-tech systems like small aerial drones and attack vessels threaten forces from the Black Sea and the Persian Gulf to the North Atlantic. Resupplying units and supporting troops elsewhere are also vulnerable.

While the trilateral agreement initially focused on nuclear-powered submarines and the industrial base, military officials in AUKUS Pillar II have expanded the focus to new and emerging robotics and autonomous technologies for undersea warfare.

Hadalus and several other UUVs developed by private industry participated in the AUKUS Pillar II “Maritime Big Play-Pacific” demonstration on Wednesday in Southern California. Hadalus spent five days at sea for the event, which included more than 40 industry and government maritime multi-domain systems.

The demonstration and live-fire operational vignettes focused on strike operations, contested resupply and undersea warfare, according to the U.S. Navy. San Diego-based Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific, U.S. Pacific Fleet and the Marine Corps hosted the event, held in San Diego, at San Clemente Island and Camp Pendleton Marine Corps Base.

Collaboration among industry and governments from all three countries is central to AUKUS to develop and field emerging technologies, officials said Wednesday during a media roundtable.

“The objective is straightforward. Identify areas where working together delivers an operational advantage that no one nation could achieve as efficiently on its own,” said Michael Dodd, assistant secretary for critical technologies in the Office of the Undersecretary for Research and Engineering at the Pentagon.

Through Maritime Big Play events, the Pentagon is bringing operators, technical experts and industry together earlier in the process, said Dodd, whose office sponsored the MBP-Pacific event.

“That ensures operational relevance and interoperability are built in from the outset of these sprints, not added after a system’s already been developed,” said Dodd. “The work is practical. It’s about evaluating systems under demanding conditions, improving interoperability in real time and identifying force multipliers that can strengthen the combined force.”

AUKUS is Making ‘Real Progress’

This year’s priorities under Pillar II are focused on torpedoes, unmanned vehicles, mines and undersea communications, Dodd said. Autonomous undersea vehicles – with the ability to deploy and employ a range of payloads in a contested logistics environment from sensors to drones and torpedoes – was the focus of MBP-Pacific. The delivery of systems and payloads is slated to start next year.

But Pillar II goes beyond demonstration, said Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the U.K.’s Special Representative for AUKUS. Pillar II is seeing experimentation and capability building, as well as improved interoperability among industry and governments.

“This is not about looking at the best of each other’s kit and systems and seeing which one to choose,” Lovegrove said. “This is about making sure that the whole thing works together, and that 1+1+1 equals considerably more than three.”

David Nockels, Australia’s first assistant secretary for Defense Trade, Regulation and Industrial Collaboration, said he’s seeing “real progress” across Pillar II.The government is developing the Royal Australian Navy’s Ghost Shark fleet in partnership with Anduril Australia. This week, military and government officials announced investments in UUV payloads, including the ability to lay sea mines and deploy drones, small and towed sonar.

“As the strategic environment becomes far more complex, the need to accelerate our delivery of military capability and strengthen interoperability is only increasing,” Nockels said. “[Lessons learned] will inform future experimentation, future capability development and the operational integration of our militaries and… help ensure AUKUS continues to deliver practical capability outcomes for our warfighters.”

In the overall scenario for the latest demonstration MBP-Pacific Pillar II, joint forces moving across island chains faced off against an adversary that impacted logistical support and resupply, said Gerry Tighe, Maritime Big Play director and former naval aviator. Enemy threats came from drones in the air, on the surface and undersea. The scenario represented “a whole new world” where using lethal systems or sensors like acoustic sonar arrays demonstrated during Pillar II can provide a warfighting advantage, Tighe said.

While this latest Pillar II scenario was set with the Indo-Pacific in mind, Pillar II’s focus on maritime capabilities is “theater agnostic,” Lovegrove said.

“We clearly are committed to playing our part in the Indo-Pacific, but our main focus is the North Atlantic, Mediterranean and High North. These are obviously areas where the principal threat is Russia,” he said. 

U.K. military officials have deemed Russia the greatest threat to U.K. security, most recently in September during a speech at the Department of Naval Research in London. First Sea Lord Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins said Russia has increased its activities in the North Atlantic and is probing the U.K. for weaknesses. The Royal Navy is spending more time and resources monitoring Russian vessels and the shadow fleet. An average of two Royal Navy warships deploy each week to conduct such tasks, Jenkins said.

“Our approach is to monitor, track and then call out the bad behavior,” Second Sea Lord Vice Adm. Paul Beattie, told reporters on Wednesday. “I think we know how important undersea cables and pipelines are to any nation, but particularly to an island nation.”

Maritime Solutions

AUKUS Pillar II provides tech companies a way to collaborate with other vendors and products, and MBP-Pacific served as a realistic venue to show their capabilities and utility to the military.

“You’ve got to be able to work together and collaborate and make a system of systems that solves the mission, rather than the one thing you’re looking at,” Rosenthal said.

CET’s fully autonomous Hadalus UUV has everything it needs to swim, navigation sensors – “everything it needs to know where it is in the world to avoid hitting anything,” Rosenthal said. 

Additionally, it can be equipped with additional systems as needed. On Wednesday, the battery-operated vehicle was outfitted with a launcher system to deploy six drums.

Hadalus’ carbon-fiber composite hull “is acoustically invisible,” Rosenthal said, its dark hue helping it blend into the sea. Over the five days Hadalus was in the water, data showed it is undetectable, according to Rosenthal. 

“It’s surprising how hard it is to spot when it’s bobbing around in the waves,” Rosenthal said. “We suspected that it would be hard to find in the water, but we didn’t have hard data to show that. Getting that data saying we truly can’t be detected was super, super beneficial.”

CET is currently capable of building 110 UUVs per month at its Rhode Island factory with the possibility of expanding to accommodate a higher production rate, Rosenthal said. The company and its partners are working through a contract with the Marine Corps for a smaller UUV.

Among UUVs in play at MBP-Pacific was Dive-XL, Anduril Australia’s extra-large autonomous undersea vehicle that fits into a standard 40-foot container. It can carry multiple payloads, including Ultra Maritime’s Sea Spear deployable acoustic array.

“You could leave this behind on the bottom and then it can detect contacts that swim by and then communicate between the different nodes,” said Tim Rochholz, Anduril Maritime’s director of fleet integration and U.S. XL programs. 

Dive-XL’s configurable bays support various payloads, including Copperhead UUVs, Mark 48 torpedo equivalents and Seabed Sentry, he said.

“The challenging part is the data,” Rochholz said. “You can collect all this data you want on the bottom of the ocean. You’ve got to get it somewhere off the ocean floor and then do something with that information.”

One U.K vendor’s system played a key role during MBP-Pacific. Seaber’s RECALL, a small orange recoverable UUV, served as the enemy in the anti-submarine warfare scenarios.

“It’s pretending to be a submarine. We were the target,” said John Peters, ocean systems technician with RS Aqua, a Portsmouth, U.K.-based company that distributes the French-made device.

The UUV has a wide range of frequencies that it can emit to mimic a range of undersea threats.

The underwater drone can reach a depth up to 300 meters. Because it is recoverable, the UUV can reduce costs with repeated use. 

Feedback from the ASW demonstrations were positive, Peters said. 

“Systems were detecting us, which is good,” he said.

Easing Barriers

Existing U.S. regulations – specifically International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR – control the sale, transfer and export of defense and military technologies that can stymie innovation and limit interoperability among industry and nations.

Easing ITAR restrictions will smooth those acquisition pathways and get systems produced and into the hands of operators more quickly, officials said. 

Some restrictions and exclusions go back decades and are still impacting systems in use during the demonstrations, Dodd said. 

“We’re trying to raise those things up to the surface so we can adjudicate them as partners and eliminate the go-slow barriers that are there,” Dodd said.

ITARis not “the sexiest thing in the world” but it is extremely important for ensuring that allied nations have the best available kit to them to meet today’s challenges,” Lovegrove said.

Developing capabilities, especially on a trilateral basis, is difficult work, he said. 

“We need to make sure that we are knocking down the bureaucratic barriers,” Lovegrove said. “That work is not complete yet, and there is still work to be done on ITAR and exempted technologies.”

Removing some barriers and licensing requirements has allowed tech companies to innovate from company to company and move at pace to develop some of these technologies without the previous regulator barriers, Nockels said.

More Fleet Capabilities, Fewer People

Military officials see autonomous systems as important augments to the fleet, including new ships and submarines. That balance is something the Royal Navy has been recalculating, according to the Second Sea Lord.

“Our aim is to take the crewed platforms and then enhance the capability of the platform in terms of the people and the ship with autonomous capabilities,” Beattie said.

The Royal Navy has the Kraken autonomous uncrewed surface vessel operationally deployed. The service is fielding that USV through a contract with U.K.-based Kraken Technology Group for 20 USVs as it shifts its fleet to a hybrid navy.

During a Tuesday display for Pillar II attendees, three aerial drones launched from a Kraken, all controlled by one person. 

“That enables us to bring mass to bear, because the cheaper systems operated by a fewer number of people means that we can gain a mass that will give us the fighting edge that we simply couldn’t achieve with crewed systems,” said Cmdr. Ed Smith, the Royal Navy’s principal warfare officer focused on the underwater environment. “There is still a requirement for human interaction in order to manage the autonomy and enable the autonomy to actually deliver the effect we properly wanted it to do.”

For anti-submarine warfare missions, autonomous systems let crews remain at safer distances. 

“If you are close to a submarine, it’s going to get you every time,” said Smith. “You want to position your assets as far away as possible whilst managing where the submarine threat is. The uncrewed assets actually enable us to get sensors closer into the submarine, enabling our decision makers to be in that proper standoff position in a way that we just cannot do with crewed systems.”

Military and industry officials touted the sheer advantages that the tech provides.

“Clearly autonomous systems are cheaper and capable of being deployed at mass and can do things that crewed systems can’t all the time, and they provide an edge on the battlefield that is apparent,” Lovegrove said.

Autonomous uncrewed systems can put combat capabilities where needed under threat, rather than people, saving lives. Used in mass at levels that crewed platforms can’t replicate provides a warfighting advantage. They can also deploy and operate for long periods, a persistence that with mass over a large area might remove the need for few, if any, humans in the danger zone.

For all the warfighting advantages, officials say autonomy won’t fully replace people.

“That’s a calculus that’s not been fully worked out yet,” said Capt. Keith Taylor, tasked with cohering autonomy and uncrewed systems for the Royal Navy’s capability directorate. 

As more uncrewed systems are fielded, Taylor said people’s roles will change.There might be fewer people at the front line in crewed ships, and a lot more people in remote operating centers.

“We are delivering capability right now. But certainly within the next five to 10 years, I would see a real shift in the balance,” Taylor said.

Each of the three countries will determine the balance of its crewed and uncrewed fleets, Lovegrove said.

“The absolute imperative [is)] that we fight together, that we have systems and tactics and procedures that allow us to go to war, to provide a deterrent effect together… and that we are moving as one,” Lovegrove said.

The following is a summary of major ship movements and exercises in the Western Pacific over the last week. 

In the Philippine Sea

The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group was in the Philippine Sea as of Wednesday as part of U.S.-Japan Exercise Keen Sword 27. 

Aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) with embarked Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 11 and cruiser USS Chosin (CG-65) is leading Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182),destroyers JS Kongo (DDG-173) and JS Asahi (DD-119), Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Stuart (FFH153), Royal Canadian frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) and a French frigate in the naval drills. 

In the Celebes Sea

The People’s Liberation Army Navy Liaoning CSG was spotted Friday transiting the Basilan Strait, which is between Basilan and Zamboanga City, Philippines. The strike group includes aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16), cruisers CNS Anshan (103) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainen (123). 

In Japan

The U.S.-Japan bilateral Exercise Keen Sword 27 is being carried out in Japan from Monday to Oct. 29. The majority of activities will take place in Japan’s southwest region. 

Approximately 45,000 Japan Self-Defense Force, 11,000 U.S. service members and forces from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines are participating alongside observers from the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom. 

A total of 260 aircraft and 40 ships, including the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group are being deployed for the drills, which opened Monday with a formal ceremony on Ishigaki Island. 

Along with at-sea drills, Marine Corps and Japan Ground Self-Defense Force (JGSDF) anti-ship and anti-air missile units will be deployed to the Sakishima Islands for island defense drills. 

Drone demonstrations will occur at Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) Iwakuni, and U.S. Air Force F-22 Raptor fighters will deploy to Japan Air Self-Defense Force Tsuiki Air Base. Airfield repair training will take place at Kadena Air Base, cyber exercises at Sagami Depot, joint fighter aircraft flights and an “elephant walk” of Marine Corps and JGSDF rotary wing and tiltrotor aircraft will be at MCAS Futenma.

In U.S. 7th Fleet

Amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island (LHD-8) is transiting the Pacific westward on deployment after a port visit to Hawaii. The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group includes Makin Island, USS Anchorage (LPD-23), USS John P. Murtha (LPD-26), and the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Destroyer USS Howard (DDG-83) is operating in the Pacific Ocean. Howard is forward-deployed to Japan and assigned to Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 15.

Amphibious transport dock USS New Orleans (LPD-18) carried out a replenishment-at-sea with Republic of Korea Navy fast combat support ship ROKS Soyang (AOE-51) on Monday. New Orleans, assigned to Expeditionary Strike Group 7, Task Force 76, is currently underway conducting routine operations in the U.S. 7th Fleet area of operations.

In Malaysia and Singapore

Five Power Defense Arrangements (FPDA) Exercise Bersama Lima concluded on Friday, having begun on Oct. 5. 

A total of 1900 personnel from Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore and the U.K. participated with seven ships, one submarine and 42 aircraft in Malaysia and Singapore. Activities included surface-to-air defense, joint urban operations, Combined Anti-Submarine Exercises (CASEX), Dissimilar Air Combat Training (DACT), Boarding Exercise and replenishment at sea. 

Naval vessels that participated included Royal Australian Navy fleet oiler HMAS Stalwart (A304), Republic of Singapore Navy frigate RSS Intrepid, littoral mission vessel RSS Dauntless (21) and an Invincible-class submarine, Royal Malaysian Navy corvette KD Lekir (FSG26) and offshore patrol vessel KD Pahang (172) and Royal Navy offshore patrol vessels HMS Tamar (P233) and HMS Spey (P234). 

The FPDA has released a video of the exercise’s highlights.

In Bayuwangi, East Java, Indonesia

Indonesia-Australia joint bilateral exercise Keris Woomera 26 concluded on Tuesday, having begun on Oct. 12. The exercise saw 1,000 Australian Defense Force personnel and more than 1,200 members of the Indonesian National Armed Forces carry out complex training across maritime, land, air and cyber domains. 

There were nine days of combined joint training in East Java, the Bali Sea and surrounding maritime areas. 

The joint naval task group included Indonesian Navy corvette KRI Sultan Iskandar Muda (367) and Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Perth (FFH157), amphibious dock landing ship HMAS Choules (L100) and fleet oiler Stalwart. The fleet oiler then moved on to Singapore for Exercise Bersama Shield.

In the South China Sea

Littoral Combat Ship USS Charleston (LCS-18) was operating near Sabina Shoal on Tuesday. The maritime feature is claimed by China. 

“The U.S. action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability. The U.S. side should immediately cease such activities,” reads a statement on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) official social media account China Military Bugle.

In Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam

Royal Navy offshore patrol vessel HMS Spey docked Friday in Nha Rong Port in Ho Chi Minh City for a port visit. Spey previously operated in the waters off Malaysia and Singapore for Five Power Defence Arrangements Exercise Bersama Lima.

In Qingdao, China

The People’s Liberation Army Navy 48th Escort Task Group arrived Friday at its homeport of Qingdao, China. The task group includes destroyer CNS Tangshan (122), CNS frigate Daqing (576) and fleet oiler CNS Taihu (889).

During its 378-day mission, the task force sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles and escorted 423 Chinese and foreign vessels in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia. The PLAN has conducted the rotational deployments of escort task groups to the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia since 2008. 

JMSDF P-1 Maritime Patrol Aircraft tracked the task group sailing northeast 220 kilometers – 137 miles – south of Miyako Island on Oct. 16 and subsequently sailing between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the East China Sea on Saturday.

In the Yellow Sea

The ROKN conducted joint and combined maritime operations training in the Yellow Sea from Tuesday to Friday as part of the larger Republic of Korea Armed Forces Hoguk annual field training exercise. The exercise will run from Monday to Oct. 30 and involves participation from U.S. forces in South Korea. 

A total of 20 ROKN surface ships – including destroyers ROKS Seoae Ryu Seong-ryong (DDG-993), ROKS Gang Gam-chan (DDH-979) and ROKS Eulji Mundeok (DDH-972) – along with U.S. and ROKN MPA and Republic of Korea Air Force fighter aircraft participated in the drills from Tuesday to Friday.

Participating forces carried out a range of drills, including maritime maneuvers, live-fire naval gunnery, maritime interdiction operations, anti-submarine warfare and combined Maritime Counter-Special Operations Force operations.

In Sasebo, Japan

JMSDF destroyer JS Kirisame (DD-104) departed Saturday from JMSDF Sasebo Naval Base for a deployment to the Gulf of Aden as the 55th Deployment Surface Force for Counter Piracy Enforcement.

The deployment is JMSDF’s ongoing rotational deployment for counter-piracy and escort missions in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia and began in 2009.

In Yokosuka, Japan

Attack submarine USS Vermont (SSN-792) docked Thursday in Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka, according to local ship spotters and a release by the Yokosuka City Council.

In the Sea of Japan

A Russian IL-20 Electronic Intelligence aircraft with tailcode RF-75936 flew over the Sea of Japan Saturday, Thursday and Friday. 

Saturday’s flight saw the aircraft fly in from the Russian continent to the waters north of Kyoto Prefecture before turning back. Thursday and Friday’s flight paths were the same, with the IL-20 flying west of Hokkaido to north of Shimane Prefecture before turning back. 

Fighter aircraft of the JASDF Northern Air Defense Command and other units were scrambled in response.

In the East China Sea

On Tuesday, a Chinese Y-9 ELINT aircraft conducted a round-trip flight from south of the Danjo Islands in the East China Sea to northwest of Okinawa before returning toward the Chinese mainland. The JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command scrambled fighter aircraft in response.

In the Osumi Strait

PLAN destroyer CNS Qiqihar (121) and fast combat support ship CNS Hulunhu (901) were sighted on Oct. 16 sailing southeast 140 kilometers –87 miles – west of Kuchinoerabu Island. On Saturday, the two ships sailed east through the Osumi Strait, which separates the main island of Kyushu and Tanegashima Island, to enter the Pacific Ocean. JMSDF frigate JS Mikuma (FFM-4) and a JMSDF P-1 MPA shadowed the PLAN ships.

 PLAN Dongdiao-class surveillance ship Yuhengxing (798) transited the Osumi Strait on Saturday and Sunday to enter the Pacific Ocean, having been sighted sailing east 100 kilometers – 62 miles – west of Kuchinoerabu Island. JMSDF multi-purpose support ship JS Amakusa (AMS-4303) and a JMSDF P-1 MPA carried out surveillance on Yuhengxing.

PLAN frigate CNS Jingzhou (532) was sighted Monday sailing east 100 kilometers – 62 miles – west of Kuchinoerabu Island. From Monday to Tuesday, the frigate sailed east through the Osumi Strait to enter the Pacific Ocean. JMSDF destroyer JS Teruzuki (DD-116) and a JMSDF Fleet Air Wing 4 P-1 MPA shadowed the PLAN frigate.

In the Miyako Strait

PLAN Dongdiao-class surveillance ship Kaiyangxing (796) was sighted Saturday sailing south 80 kilometers – 50 miles – northwest of Kume Island and subsequently sailed south between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. A JMSDF P-1 of Fleet Air Wing 1 carried out surveillance on the PLAN ship.

On Monday, one Chinese military BZK-005 Unmanned Aerial Vehicle and a Chinese Y-9 ELINT aircraft flew from the East China Sea, passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea and carried out a circuit flight before returning back to the East China Sea. Fighter aircraft from the JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command were scrambled in response.

On Tuesday, a Chinese Y-9 MPA flew from the East China Sea and passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. After flying as far off the island of Amami Oshima, the aircraft turned back and passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the East China Sea and returned to China. The JASDF scrambled fighter aircraft from the Southwestern Air Defense Command in response.

On Wednesday, a Chinese Y-9 ELINT from the East China Sea entered the Philippine Sea after passing between Okinawa and Miyako Island. After flying as far as the island of Amami Oshima, the aircraft turned back and passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to return to the East China Sea. The JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command scrambled fighter aircraft in response.

Near Taiwan

On Monday, a Chinese TB-001 UAV flew in from the East China Sea and passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan to enter the Philippine Sea where it flew as far as the island of Amami Oshima before turning back and returning to the East China Sea. The JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command scrambled fighter aircraft in response.

At Fleet Base East, Australia

Destroyer HMAS Sydney (DDG42) returned home to Fleet Base East, New South Wales on Saturday, following 131 days operating across the Indo-Pacific. The deployment included participation in exercises Rim of the Pacific and Pacific Dragon in Hawaii and Pacific Vanguard and Nichi-Gou Trident in the waters of Guam.

At Devonport Naval Base, New Zealand

The Royal New Zealand Navy Task Group – frigate HMNZS Te Mana (F111) and fleet oiler HMNZS Aotearoa (A11) – arrived home in Devonport Naval Base on Friday, completing a 134-day deployment that included participation in RIMPAC and monitoring North Korean maritime sanctions evasion.

This post was written by Dzirhan Mahadzir.

The U.S. Army’s recently activated a Guam-based air defense battalion meant to protect the island from increasingly advanced air and missile threats fielded by China and North Korea. 

The 3rd Battalion, 43rd Air Defense Artillery Regiment, activated on Oct. 16, will inherit the defense of Guam responsibilities of Task Force Talon. The previous Army rotational mission began in 2013 to counter potential North Korean ballistic missile threats. 

With the rise of the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force in recent years, the mission has expanded its focus to defend against a barrage of Chinese missiles in a potential conflict. The Pentagon initiated plans for the Guam Defense System in 2023 to meet the requirements needed to defeat Beijing’s ballistic, cruise and hypersonic strikes. 

“Guam’s strategic location makes it an important part of U.S. military operations throughout the region by supporting joint force operations while making air and missile defense a critical part of protecting the forces and infrastructure needed to support those missions,” reads the Army release on the battalion’s activation. 

The ground branch has eyed a reinforced posture on Guam with the increase of Indo-Pacific adversaries’ long-range precision strike capabilities. The 3-43 ADA will operate Patriot, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense and new Intermediate Fires Protection Capability systems, Stars and Stripes reported in August. Compared to the legacy Patriot and THAAD systems, IFPC will provide medium- to short-range defense against aircraft, missiles and drones. 

When combined, the systems provide a layered network to engage a variety of air and missile threats that could be fielded in a potential Western Pacific conflict. 

“The soldiers developed new procedures, relationships and integration required to connect sensors, command and control systems, launchers and interceptors to promote a unified defensive architecture. It’s only fitting that 3-43 ADA now stands up the Army’s contribution to the strategic Guam Defense System,” Lt. Col. Joshua Urness, 3-43 ADA BN commander, said in the release. 

According to the Army, the transition from task force to battalion signals the Defense Department’s commitment “toward permanent air defense capabilities in the Indo-Pacific.”

Guam’s current air defenses are composed of six Army THAAD launchers and U.S. Navy Aegis Combat System warships assigned to its defense on an as-need basis. Future plans aim to integrate a networked system capable of conducting 360-degree detection and interception of air and missile threats. 

Since Task Force Talon’s original mission over a decade ago, the complexity and quantity of Indo-Pacific missile threats has only increased. Today, the People’s Liberation Army Navy is in the process of fielding more nuclear attack boats equipped with vertical launching systems. The Pentagon has also said it expects the PLAN to have a nine carrier strike group force by 2035, which will expand Beijing’s blue water projection capabilities.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — October has had the highest number of ship attacks since the war between Iran and the U.S. began in late February. 

There have been 27 attacks on commercial ships so far in October, according to the International Maritime Organization. There were 22 in March, as well as attacks on an offshore rig and two tugs, according to a list of attacks compiled by USNI News. 

Despite the number of attacks, ships are continuing to sail through the strait. There were 104 non-Iranian-linked vessels that sailed through between Oct. 5-11, during which there were 12 attacks, according to data from London-based maritime intelligence firm Lloyd’s List. Of those, six occurred on Oct. 11, according to the IMO.

Transits did fall, going from 126 the week prior. However, transits between Oct. 5-11 were still 31 percent higher than August’s weekly average, according to Lloyd’s List. 

While Iran is at fault for the majority of attacks, the U.S. has disabled a number of ships as part of its two-part blockade. 

Iran is not going after specific ships, Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told an audience at Lloyd’s List Outlook Forum on Wednesday in New York. But Iran does not have to hit every ship or a specific company to keep the risk high, Raydan said. 

“The aim is to hit as much as they can and make sure that they keep the southern route appear very unsafe and keep the risks very high,” Raydan said. 

To achieve that goal, Iran can hit one or two ships, hail another one and make them turn around or keep another in the Persian Gulf. That all keeps the risks high for vessels, she said. 

Raydan said she considers October’s number of attacks as evidence of what Iran can still do eight months into the war. 

“And I believe they are conserving some of their cards or energy for a future conflict in the region,” she said. 

Iran doesn’t need a nuclear weapon to have leverage, Joshua Tallis, a naval analyst with CNA, said during the forum. Instead, Iran can use the Strait of Hormuz as a negotiating tool. 

The strait gives Iran a lever to pull with smaller moral and social costs than a nuclear weapon, and that was something the U.S. and Iran learned as a result of the war, he said. 

“There’s no way of putting that cat back in the bag,” Tallis said. 

Iran is fighting an economic war with the U.S. by attacking ships in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, which drives up the prices of diesel and other refined oil products like gasoline. Iran knows that the US is facing a midterm and the Middle East country wants to keep those prices up in order to ship voters against the Trump administration, Tallis said. 

“What Iran is trying to do is shape market behavior, to drive costs up, to put pressure on – predominantly – the United States because the U.S. is going to be more cost sensitive, particularly in the run to earn election, where it turns out Midwestern voters care a lot about the price of diesel,” he said. 

There are no alternative routes from the Strait of Hormuz in terms of moving the same amount of oil, Tallis said. While Saudi Arabia did shift to a pipeline that uses the Red Sea as a port, Saudi Arabia had to stop using the route due to Houthi attacks. 

The pipelines are going to be just as vulnerable as ships, Tallis said, noting that the use of cheap one-way attack drones pose a problem for land structures as much as they do for vessels on the water. 

“At the end of the day, I think Iran has ratcheted the pressure up so high that it’s actually shifted the entire market incentive for commercial operators. They are now willing to take risks,” Tallis said. “The question is how much more do they need to strike?”

The U.S. reinstated its blockade on ships traveling to and from Iranian ports in July, using warships to disable tankers that violate it. The Navy has also used air defense over the Strait of Hormuz to protect commercial ships from being targeted by Iranian projectiles. 

To support U.S. operations against Iran, the Navy has maintained a two-carrier presence in the Arabian Sea for six months, according to the USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker. Additionally, an Amphibious Ready Group embarked with a Marine Expeditionary Unit has been on station in the Middle East since early March, and more than a dozen independent deployers have surged to the region. 

The U.S. can continue to hold its blockade indefinitely, Tallis told the audience. For the U.S. it is not the immediate cost that they need to be considering, but rather the long-term effect of using so many ships in the Middle East.

Every ship that has multiple extensions will require more maintenance when it returns, affecting maintenance cycles and when the ship might be ready to sail again. The U.S. is also pulling ships from the western Pacific to meet the needs in the Middle East, which affects potential future conflicts, Tallis said.

The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group, as well as Japanese, Australian, Canadian and French warships, have gathered in the Philippine Sea to participate in exercise Keen Sword 27.

The Theodore Roosevelt CSG steamed alongside ships from the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Royal Australian Navy, Royal Canadian Navy and French Navy on Wednesday in the Philippine Sea, according to a Pentagon imagery release. The imagery shows flagship USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) and USS Chosin (CG-65) sailing with JMSDF helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182) and destroyers JS Kongo (DDG-173) and destroyer JS Asahi (DD-119), RAN frigate HMAS Stuart (FFH153), RCN frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) and a French frigate.

The Theodore Roosevelt CSG includes aircraft carrier Theodore Roosevelt with embarked Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 11, cruiser Chosin, and destroyer USS Decatur (DDG-73). The strike group pulled into Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka (CFAY) on Friday for a port visit, departing on Monday.

The 10-day exercise began Monday and runs through Oct. 29.

Approximately 45,000 Japan Self-Defense Force personnel are taking part in Keen Sword alongside 11,000 U.S. troops and forces from other partner and allied nation forces, according to a U.S. Navy news release. The exercise will include 260 aircraft and 40 ships, including the Theodore Roosevelt CSG. Personnel from Australia, Canada, France, New Zealand and the Philippines are participating in the exercise, with observers from the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom.

On Tuesday, U.S. Navy Capt. Edward McLellan, commander of Information Warfare Squadron (IWRON) 9, met JMSDF and RAN personnel aboard Theodore Roosevelt, according to the U.S. Navy news release. IWRON is a new U.S. Navy unit designed to integrate information warfare capabilities. Its primary purpose is to provide a decision-making advantage to carrier strike group commanders by unifying information warfare functions into a single, accountable commander.

McLellan discussed this new approach to information warfare with his counterparts as part of the broader effort to align how the U.S. and its allies fight in the information domain. JMSDF sailors are also embarked on the carrier to observe flight deck operations.

The 12th Marine Littoral Regiment and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Western Army are carrying out synchronized expeditionary advanced base operations across Japan’s southwest islands. The Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s C-2 and C-130 aircraft are transporting U.S. Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) mobile short-range air defense and anti-drone system, the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) missile system and the TPS-80 Ground/Air Task Oriented Radars (GATOR) to the Sakishima Islands to participate in the exercise.

“By utilizing Japanese strategic transport to position mobile U.S. rocket systems, missile launchers, and air-defense radars at key maritime chokepoints, this evolution validated our combined ability to rapidly project a lethal, integrated stand-in force to defend the region and secure remote islands,” reads the release.

U.S. troops from Marine Wing Support Squadron 172 and the U.S. Air Force 18th Wing, and members from the JGSDF worked together to perform rapid airfield damage repair at Kadena Air Base on Okinawa on Tuesday. Leveraging both manual and machine tactics from the two nations, U.S. and Japanese partners are training to expedite processes that would individually take much longer. By sharing and integrating tactics, equipment, manpower and materials, the combined forces are working to develop new ways to approach the critical mission of airfield damage repair under contested conditions, reads the release.

U.S. Air Force F-22 Raptors fighters assigned to the 525th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron deployed to JASDF Tsuiki Air Base, Japan, as part of Keen Sword to conduct joint fighter training. Other U.S. aircraft arriving in Japan for Keen Sword 27 include KC-135 Stratotankers and a C-130J Super Hercules.

Air combat training is also being conducted in a hybrid format that combines both virtual and live elements for a defensive counter-air demonstration that links U.S. virtual F-35 Lightning II fighter simulators with live Japanese F-35 fighters and E-2 airborne early-warning aircraft. Enabled by the Pacific Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Capability, the event allowed allied forces to form a shared tactical scenario while operating across separate live and simulated environments.

“The deployment of these cutting-edge warfighting technologies as part of Keen Sword 27 is part of the larger objective of familiarizing U.S. and Japanese allies with each others’ equipment, tactics and procedures to enhance U.S.-Japanese interoperability, information sharing and defensive coordination across domains under realistic training conditions,” reads the release.

Meanwhile, Chinese drones were operating in Japan’s southwest region on Monday, where part of the Keen Sword drills are taking place, Japan Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tuesday during a regular press release. One Chinese BZK-005 military reconnaissance Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and a Y-9 Electronic Intelligence (ELINT) aircraft flew in from the East China Sea and passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. Later, the drone and aircraft passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island.

Additionally on Monday, a Chinese TB-001 military reconnaissance/attack UAV flew in from the East China Sea and passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan to enter the Philippine Sea. The drone flew as far as the waters off the island of Amami Oshima, and then passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the East China Sea.

Drone activity around Japan has intensified in recent years with 23 Chinese military drone incidents in Japan’s Fiscal Year 2024, approximately three times the eight incidents reported in Fiscal Year 2023, Koizumi said. A total of 16 incidents were reported in FY2025.

“This recent drone incident clearly demonstrates the need to adapt to new methods of warfare and to address the threat posed by drones. We intend to carefully explain these changes in the security environment to the public and seek their understanding,” said Koizumi.

When asked whether the Chinese Y-9 and UAVs were conducting surveillance on the Keen Sword drills, Koizumi said that in dealing with parties whose intentions are uncertain to assess, assumptions should not be made.

“We must approach such situations with caution – questioning even our own initial impressions and conduct a calm, objective analysis and assessment. For now, we have made the facts public, specifically, that these incidents, including the flight of unmanned aerial vehicles, have occurred,” Koizumi said.

He said the information was disclosed to foster public understanding of the current situation as it underscores the necessity of developing Japan’s defense capabilities.
